title: A subagent's result is not the run's terminal result
description:
Run run-841f5ee1866addb533c02a30e67f001a for yoyodyne-ifd.60 died on the second-terminal-result guard while its developer was mid-sentence resolving the last review findings. The developer had spawned Claude Code subagents (system task_started/task_notification events precede it), and a subagent's completion arrives in the parent stream as another type:result envelope -- event 1185 in the recorded stream: empty result text, empty terminal_reason, is_error false -- which the guard from the earlier parser fix reads as a forbidden second terminal result.

The guard was built when no harness developer used subagents; the first one that did lost its run at the finish line, after two repair attempts, with the third attempt's work complete in the worktree.

P0 because subagent use is the model's choice, not the bead's: any run can hit this at any time.
design: Distinguish the run's terminal result from a nested one by shape rather than order: the recorded fixture shows the subagent envelope carries no terminal_reason and no result text, while every genuine terminal carries terminal_reason and usage. Treat a result envelope without those marks as stream noise to record, not a terminal to act on -- same philosophy as the trailing-events fix: guard the invariant (one acted-on terminal), not the surface (one envelope of a type). Replay the exact recorded stream as the regression test. Note the shape on ifd.32 as more provider dialect: nested agent results are something the plugin contract must name.
acceptance_criteria: A stream containing subagent result envelopes completes normally with the parent terminal honored; the recorded run-841f5ee1 stream replays green; a genuine duplicate terminal is still rejected; the envelope shape is noted on ifd.32; no other guard weakens.

title: Rewrite the README opening: problem first, and call it yoyo
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-18, after reviewing candidate openings: direction B, problem-first. The approved opening, verbatim, is the constraint:

'Writing code was never the hard part. Deciding what to build, keeping every change traceable to why, and making sure something other than the author reviewed it before it landed -- that is the work still done by hand around every coding agent. Yoyo is that structure, built to run without you driving each turn: goals in, merged software out, a conversation to steer it.'

And the product is referred to as yoyo in the README's prose, matching the command people actually type. The current opening's defect, named by the operator: 'turns a conversation into merged code' swaps the input for the interface -- it turns goals into code, and the conversation is how the user interacts with those goals.
design:
Structure after the opening: the why-paragraph draws on the brief's own reasoning; the gates become three short bullets (nothing merges unreviewed; the reviewer runs toolless and cannot be talked into a merge; the written goals are the only authority work traces to); the conversation is presented as how you drive it rather than what it is; quick start; the existing honest-bounds section survives as is.

Naming discipline: yoyo in prose; the module path, repository name, and formal references stay Yoyodyne. The naming is settled by the operator, 2026-08-18: the product is called yoyo everywhere in prose because it reads better; yoyodyne remains the project name -- repository, module path, releases, and formal references. No question remains to raise; the brief's prose adopts the same rule in a separate operator-directed change, not in this item, because the brief is not this item's to edit. Every claim must still be true of the current build; the never-ahead-of-reality rule from the last rewrite stands.
acceptance_criteria: The README opens with the approved problem-first text; the product is yoyo in prose with formal names untouched; the gates read as three bullets; the bounds section survives; nothing contradicts the brief, the goals, or the configuration guide; the naming rule -- product yoyo, project yoyodyne -- is applied consistently in the README.

title: Show the product manager the shipped surface, labeled as description rather than intent
description: The product manager's evidence is the specifications under docs/product plus Beads state, deliberately narrowed by yoyodyne-ifd.20 after a stale README sentence was reported to the operator as current product fact. The cost surfaced 2026-08-18: the product manager did not know bin/yoyo-status or yoyo cost existed until the operator described them, a work-item draft mis-assumed which surfaces existed, and a format question about two real outputs could not be evaluated by the role deciding it. Add to the product manager's briefing a read-only section carrying the operator-facing documentation - README, docs/configuration.md, and command help - labeled as what the product ships today: description of implementation as built, never authority about intent. Done means the product manager can say what user-facing surfaces exist without the operator supplying it; the section's label states it describes what is built and that the specifications remain the sole authority on intent; a conflict between the two is something the product manager reports rather than resolves silently; and yoyodyne-ifd.20's recorded trade is revisited and its reasoning re-recorded openly rather than silently reversed. Source code, the design document, and command execution remain outside the product manager's evidence; this adds documentation of the shipped surface, nothing else.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 32.

Reason: Proposed by the product manager and approved by the operator 2026-08-18, with an explicit instruction to prioritize it: it runs as soon as the two runs now in flight settle. Priority 0 is what makes that true - the ready work it must outrank sits at priority 1, and its only p0 neighbor, yoyodyne-ifd.1, is a decomposed container whose children carry its execution. The item serves the autonomy goal by keeping the operator's routine interface able to answer surface questions without the operator standing in as its eyes, which happened twice in one day.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Give the backlog owner a live survey, and say when a tracker action touches a closed item
description:
The product manager ordered the backlog from a stale picture. Turn 19 of the 2026-08-18 conversation moved yoyodyne-ifd.23 down-tier citing yoyodyne-ifd.41 as in progress -- both had been closed for hours. Its per-item reads are live, but the open-items survey it reasons from is the one gathered when the conversation opened, external changes never reach a running conversation, and the role that owns backlog ordering is exactly the role that cannot afford a stale list. The harness also applied the priority change to the closed item without a word.

Two fixes. First, a survey tracker action, so the product manager can ask for the current open list mid-conversation the way it already reads single items -- ordering decisions then start from a fresh list as a matter of discipline stated in the persona. Second, act-time honesty: a tracker action whose target's status changed since the conversation's picture of it -- above all one targeting a closed item -- is applied only if still meaningful and its result says plainly what the target's current status is, so reasoning built on a stale premise is corrected at the moment it acts rather than never.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can request a current backlog survey mid-conversation as a tracker action; the persona directs ordering decisions to start from one; a tracker action on a closed or changed item reports the item's current status in its applied summary; a priority change on a closed item is either refused or applied with the closure stated, never silent; a test replays the ifd.23 case and the reply visibly learns the item is closed.

title: Give product and design artifacts stable identity and metadata
description:
Product and design artifacts have no stable identity. docs/product/brief.md, the goals, the non-goals, docs/designs/, and docs/decisions/ are ordinary Markdown; nothing can reference one durably, so no relationship between them can be validated. Define the identity and metadata schema those artifacts carry: a stable id, an artifact kind, a lifecycle status, and the references the artifact makes upstream.

CONSTRAINT: follow the model yoyodyne-ifd.17 already shipped for invariants rather than inventing a second scheme - the filename is the id, a frontmatter id that disagrees is refused, status is explicit, and changes append to a revision log. Two identity schemes in one repository is the failure to design against. Do not reword any document's prose; this adds identity to what exists. The brief and goals are the product manager's and the operator writes them, so a change to their content is out of scope here even where the metadata sits in the same file.

DONE: an artifact in docs/product, docs/designs, or docs/decisions carries a stable id and metadata validated on load; a malformed or duplicate id is refused with a message naming the file; docs/configuration.md documents the schema.

DECOMPOSITION NOTE: created by the product manager under operator authorization 2026-08-17, because no development manager exists yet - the role arrives with yoyodyne-ifd.4, which yoyodyne-ifd.1 gates. Decomposition belongs to the development manager; this shape should be re-derived or ratified when the role runs.
notes:
Shape check the product manager's warning asked for, done 2026-08-17 by the operator's agent, which can read the design document: the nine children were compared against Milestone 2 verbatim. All seven enumerated capabilities map to a child (IDs 1.1, relationship validation 1.2, role ownership 1.4, change proposals 1.5, staleness 1.6, directive reconciliation 1.7, approvals 1.8), seeding maps to 1.9, and 1.3 is a justified addition from the backlog audit. Two nuances, not gaps: 1.8 covers the durable approval record because the configurable half of approvals already shipped; and Milestone 2 seeds 'brief, goals, and designs' while 1.9 names product and decision artifacts -- the designs home does not exist yet, so whoever builds 1.9 should either create docs/designs/ under the settled ownership or state why seeding defers it.

title: Fix the worktree test that fails its own cleanup
description:
TestManagerIntegrateRefusesNonFastForwardAndKeepsHarnessCommit fails intermittently in CI during teardown, not assertion: 'TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat .../repository/.git: directory not empty'. Its checks pass; Go's t.TempDir cleanup then races something still holding or repopulating the repository directory, most likely a git worktree registration or a background git process that has not exited.

Observed on pull request 13 (run 31992104553) for yoyodyne-ifd.21, where it blocked the merge. The same commit passed the harness's own make test, make race and make vet, so this reproduces in CI and not locally.

P0 because build is a required status check on a protected main: a test that fails intermittently in teardown blocks every publication, and the harness cannot merge past it. It also teaches the wrong lesson -- a red required check that is usually spurious is one people stop reading.
design:
Make the test responsible for what it created rather than leaving it to TempDir. A worktree the test registered should be removed by the test before cleanup runs, and any git invocation it started should be waited for, so the directory is genuinely idle when Go tries to delete it.

Prefer fixing the leak to retrying the deletion. A cleanup that retries until the directory goes quiet hides whichever handle is still open, and that handle is the interesting thing: if a git process outlives the call that started it, the harness has the same problem outside tests.

Check the sibling tests in internal/gitworktree for the same shape before assuming this one is unique. The failure is timing-dependent, so the one that fails is not necessarily the only one that can.
acceptance_criteria: The test cleans up the worktrees and processes it creates so TempDir removal has nothing to race; it passes repeatedly under CI conditions, including with -count high enough to expose the race; no cleanup step retries deletion to paper over a held handle; sibling tests with the same pattern are corrected too.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 when it blocked pull request 13 and stalled the queue. Rerunning the job cleared it, which is the symptom of a flake rather than a fix.

title: Queue the merge with --auto so required checks are waited for
description:
Publishing merges the moment the reviewer approves, but a protected branch will not accept a merge until its required checks have passed. CI takes about forty seconds and the harness asks within seconds of approving, so the merge is refused on essentially every run.

Observed on the first published run, run-ab96b7a966d3b718dc9287d9f5846725 for yoyodyne-ifd.20.1. The run succeeded, the reviewer approved, the work integrated locally and pull request 5 opened, and the merge was refused: 'the base branch's protection rules are not satisfied (BLOCKED) ... the base branch policy prohibits the merge.' GitHub's own message names the remedy: add --auto to have the pull request merged once the requirements are met.

Nothing is lost when this happens -- the outcome is reported as 'the change is integrated locally; the pull request still needs to be reconciled by hand' -- but it leaves an open pull request and an unpushed local branch after every run, which is precisely the manual reconciliation that publishing exists to remove.
design:
Ask GitHub to merge when the requirements are met rather than asking it to merge now. gh pr merge --auto queues the merge and lets the forge complete it once required checks pass, which is what a protected branch is asking for.

Auto-merge is a repository setting, so it can be unavailable. Detect that and say so plainly rather than failing obscurely: a repository with auto-merge disabled and required checks configured cannot be published to this way, and the operator should be told which setting to change.

Do not reach for --admin. Merging with administrator privileges bypasses the very checks the protection expresses, and a harness that routinely overrides branch protection has removed the gate rather than satisfied it.

The confirmation loop needs rethinking alongside this. It currently asks three times over seven seconds whether the merge landed, which suited an immediate merge and cannot suit a queued one. A queued merge completes minutes later, so the run should record the pull request as queued and finish, rather than waiting for something that will not happen while it watches. What reconciliation does about a queued merge that later fails is the open question worth answering here.
acceptance_criteria: A merge into a protected branch with required checks succeeds without manual reconciliation; the harness queues the merge rather than demanding it immediately; a repository that cannot auto-merge is reported with the setting that needs changing rather than a generic refusal; administrator override is never used to bypass protection; a run whose merge is queued finishes and reports the pull request as queued rather than blocking on a confirmation that cannot arrive; reconciliation defines what happens to a queued merge that later fails.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 on the first run after enabling branch protection and approvals.publishing. P0 because it affects every published run and reintroduces the manual step publishing was meant to remove.

title: Do not discard a completed run over provider output after the terminal result
description:
internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go rejects any line arriving after the provider's terminal result envelope: ParseLine returns 'provider event received after terminal result' as a fatal error. The Claude Code CLI does emit trailing events after its result, so a run whose developer finished successfully is thrown away.

Observed on run-44a559a57d3710e6cd99125efd29ee2d for yoyodyne-ifd.12. The developer completed and emitted its final summary at sequence 586; the run then failed with that parse error, discarding 975 insertions of finished work that never reached checks or review. The error repeated three times in the output, so more than one trailing event arrived.

This is a reliability defect affecting every run, not a problem specific to that work item, which is why it is P0: any run can complete its work and then be discarded for output the provider legitimately emits. It also interacts with yoyodyne-ifd.12, since a rate-limit notice is one of the things plausibly arriving late.
design:
A terminal result means the run's outcome is decided; it does not mean the provider stops writing. Record events that arrive after it rather than failing on them, and keep the already-decided result. Guard the actual invariant, which is that a second terminal result must not silently replace the first, rather than treating all trailing output as corruption.

Preserve what the trailing events carry instead of discarding it. They are exactly where a late rate-limit notice would appear, and yoyodyne-ifd.12 needs that payload. Do not let a post-terminal event mutate the recorded result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, or cost, since those belong to the terminal envelope; append them to the event stream so they remain diagnosable.
acceptance_criteria: A provider event arriving after the terminal result no longer fails the run; the terminal result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, and cost are unchanged by anything arriving after it; trailing events appear in the recorded event stream; a second terminal result is still rejected rather than replacing the first; a test replays a stream with events after the result and asserts the run succeeds with the original outcome intact.

title: Retry the worktree listing that crosses a half-written creation
description: Third member of the worktree race family: git worktree add registers its entry under .git/worktrees before filling it in, and a 'git worktree list --porcelain' that reads the entry in between fails the whole command, so a run can be lost to nothing but another run starting beside it. The creation lease (ifd.71) cannot cover this: a creation holds the lease while verifying what it just made — which is itself a listing — so a listing waiting on the lease would wait for itself. The fix is a bounded re-read (only a Git that ran and refused is retried; a Git that could not run or timed out is not). A complete, tested implementation already exists: run-0c561cc3's preserved branch (yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-70/0c561cc3) carries it in internal/gitworktree/manager.go and manager_test.go (+52/+146); ifd.70's reviewer refused it only as out of scope for a reports item, not on the merits. title: Fence worktree pruning: git auto-maintenance can delete a registration mid-creation
description: ifd.71's creation lease serializes the harness's own git worktree add calls, but nothing fences git worktree prune, and Git's auto-maintenance (gc --auto) prunes worktrees inside managed repositories after ordinary write commands. A registration still being created has no index file yet, so a prune can judge it stale and delete it mid-creation; the developer reproduced the failure racing a prune against concurrent adds on git 2.50.1, and the reviewer notes any concurrent removal presents the same partially-deleted-entry class of exit-128 failure to an in-flight add. Candidate fixes: extend the ifd.71 lease to cover the harness's own removals, and disable auto-gc/prune in harness-managed repositories (gc.auto=0 or maintenance settings) or take the lease around any command that can trigger it. Reported by ifd.71's developer and reviewer; the PM should judge whether this joins the v0.2.0 gates or ships behind them.

title: Serialize git worktree add: concurrent creates can lose a run to half-written bookkeeping
description: gitworktree.Manager.Create runs git worktree add unserialized, and two at the same instant against one repository can fail: one add reads the other's half-written .git/worktrees/<name>/commondir and exits 128 ('failed to read ... commondir'). Production exposure is real wherever max_concurrent_developers > 1, which is this repository's own configuration. Fix in the manager (serialize creation per repository, or retry on the known transient failure), then remove the test mutex so the suite exercises the real path. title: Goal statements wrapped across lines are silently recorded as their first fragment
description: The goals parser records one physical line per goal statement. A goal written the way Markdown is normally written — hard-wrapped at 80 columns — is silently truncated to its first line: yoyo goals list prints a fragment, and attribution against the full statement fails with 'no goal recorded in v1-goals is stated in those words'. This bit the legibility goal (fixed by rejoining it onto one line, PR #59), and the product manager could not diagnose it because she cannot read files; the failure named the words she used, not the truncation. Either unwrap continuation lines (a bullet's indented following lines belong to the statement, up to the italic Supports trailer) or refuse a wrapped goal loudly at load. Silent truncation is the one wrong option: for anyone with a repo whose editor wraps Markdown, every goal corrupts at once.
notes:
The product manager recorded this same defect as design context on yoyodyne-ifd.43 (document shape contract). This bead is the concrete parser fix; reconcile with ifd.43's design when that item is taken up.
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 64.

title: The product manager briefs like an executive assistant: short context, one question at a time
description:
Operator instruction, 2026-08-18, about behavior that is obvious on first contact: the product manager answers with walls of text carrying several questions at once. It should treat the operator like a CEO -- brief context first, an offer to expand rather than the expansion, and exactly one question per turn. When it holds several, it opens with the count and its ordering: 'I have n questions; I'll ask them in order of <importance / which answers would change the later questions>' and then asks the first.

This is the discipline the operator's own agent has used on them all week, one question at a time, and the operator has repeatedly chosen it.
design:
Persona guidance, not contract: how a role phrases things is a project's to override, so it lands in the product-manager persona -- both the builtin template and this repository's copied personas/product-manager.md, which are now independent after the explicit-configuration change and must both be edited.

The shape to state: lead with the conclusion or the ask in a sentence or two; offer depth ('say more if you want the reasoning') instead of front-loading it; one question per reply, carrying its stakes -- what the answer unblocks -- so the operator can answer or defer knowingly; several questions get the count-and-ordering preamble, and the ordering criterion is named, preferring answers that would change later questions. A blocking concern under the validation rules stays a question that stops and waits; this shapes its form, not its force.

The first-contact case matters most: the blank-repository opening from the goals-prompt work asks what the product is, who it is for, and what finished means -- three questions that must now arrive as a count, an order, and the first question, not a paragraph containing all three.
acceptance_criteria: Product-manager replies lead with brief context and an explicit offer to expand; no reply carries more than one question; multiple pending questions produce a count and a named ordering, then the first; the blank-repository opening follows the same discipline; both persona copies carry the guidance; the conversation record shows the behavior on a real first-run transcript.
notes:
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 44.

Reason: The product manager's briefing style is the routine interface this goal names, working well or badly: one question at a time with stakes attached is what makes stating intent and answering escalations tolerable as the human's whole surface. The first-contact case the item calls out - the blank-repository opening - is the interface's first impression.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

Operator directive, 2026-08-18, add to the persona guidance this item lands: be concise and treat every word as scarce. No ornament or figurative filler ('the pen is out' was the example corrected). Plain statements, nothing that carries no value.

title: Have yoyo init propose the project's checks instead of leaving a blank to fill
description:
Operator reaction, 2026-08-18, reading the README's adoption line 'bd init && yoyo init # then write your project's checks into .yoyodyne/config.yaml': what are the checks, do I need to do something by hand?! The three-step spine -- install, init, chat -- currently breaks at a hand-edited YAML list, the only manual edit in the flow.

The repository already announces its toolchain. init should read what is there and propose checks: a Makefile's test/check targets, go.mod (go test ./...), package.json scripts (npm test, tsc where present), pyproject/pytest, gradle/maven wrappers. Proposals, not guesses installed silently: written into config.yaml as the checks list when the detection is confident, with a comment naming what they were derived from, and as commented candidates with a clear you-must-choose marker when it is not. A repository where nothing is detected keeps today's placeholder plus a pointer at the configuration guide's per-language examples.
design: Detection is by artifact presence only -- no command is executed during init, because running a stranger's build to discover it is not a first impression. Keep the language-agnostic invariant intact: this adds convenience defaults derived from the project's own files, not toolchain understanding in the harness; the run path stays exit-codes-only. init --json reports what was detected and what was written so the walkthrough script can assert it. The README's adoption line then drops the hand-edit comment where detection succeeded and says review the proposed checks instead.
acceptance_criteria: init on a Go, Node, Python, or Make-based repository writes runnable proposed checks with their provenance commented; ambiguous detection produces commented candidates and an explicit marker rather than silent guesses; no project command executes during init; empty detection preserves today's behavior; the README adoption path reflects it; the adoption walkthrough exercises detection on its non-Go fixture.

title: One switch to pause all harness activity
description:
Operator instruction, 2026-08-18: a mechanism to quickly pause all activity -- to conserve tokens, or for any other reason -- and resume it later.

Today there is no such verb. Stopping things means killing processes, which the manual release taught lands as terminal cancelled runs with claimed items and lost work; the only clean pauses are the ones providers impose.
design:
A durable pause flag in the state root, set and cleared by operator verbs (yoyo pause / yoyo resume), honored at every provider-call boundary: a developer attempt, a reviewer invocation, a conversation turn, and any future scheduler claim checks it before spending a token. An in-flight run that reaches a boundary while paused parks exactly as it parks for a usage limit -- durable, resumable, budget-accounted under its own named kind (operator_hold) so the ledger shows why time passed -- and the probe discipline from ifd.53 picks the flag up: probes see the hold and keep waiting without cost, resume clears it and the next probe proceeds. This is deliberately the same waiting machinery as limits and overloads, not a third mechanism: an operator hold is one more waitable condition, with the operator as its reset.

Honest boundary: a generation already streaming is not interrupted; pause takes effect at the next call. Say so. yoyo-status and the conversation /status lead with a PAUSED banner while the flag is set, because a system the operator paused and forgot looks exactly like a system that died.

Relation recorded: ifd.26 names pause-intake versus stop-everything as distinct intentions for the management hierarchy; this is the role-independent floor under both, and ifd.26 builds its finer controls on top rather than replacing it.
acceptance_criteria: yoyo pause causes every subsequent provider-call boundary to park instead of spending; in-flight runs pause durably and resume unaided after yoyo resume; conversation turns refuse or hold with the reason stated; paused time is accounted under an operator-hold kind distinct from provider limits; yoyo-status and /status show the paused state prominently; a stream already in flight completes and the boundary behavior is documented; kill remains unnecessary.
notes:
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 44.

Reason: The override clause again, one level broader than ifd.53: a durable operator hold honored at every provider-call boundary is recovery and override made available without killing processes, and the item records the relation to ifd.26's finer controls explicitly - this is the role-independent floor under them. Autonomy the operator cannot cheaply pause is autonomy working against its owner.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Scale the check timeout to the work, and make it configurable
description:
Soak finding, 2026-08-18: with two developers running concurrently, run-af68c66fe3ba77e0243cbf32aed24ae0 for yoyodyne-ifd.1.7 finished development and its tests were passing package by package when make test hit the checks runner's flat ten-minute default timeout (internal/checks/runner.go defaultTimeout) under CPU contention, failing a run whose work was good. The suite has grown past forty packages with real git-repository integration tests; two concurrent suites contend for the same cores.

The Timeout field exists on the runner and nothing wires it from configuration.
design: Make the per-check timeout configurable (execution.check_timeout or per-check), keep a sane default with headroom above the observed single-run suite time, and state the concurrency interaction honestly in the configuration guide: N concurrent runs multiply suite wall clock, so the timeout should scale or the checks should serialize. Consider reporting elapsed-vs-timeout on every check so growth toward the ceiling is visible before it bites, consistent with the stalled-provider lesson: a timeout that kills passing work is the wall-clock mistake again, one layer down.
acceptance_criteria: The check timeout is configurable and documented with its concurrency interaction; the default clears the current suite under two concurrent runs; a check that times out reports elapsed and limit; a passing suite under contention completes.
notes:
Yoyodyne run passed checks, was approved by an independent reviewer, and was integrated automatically.

title: Wait out a transient server overload instead of failing the run
description:
Two runs failed instantly on 2026-08-18 with API Error: 529 Overloaded -- the provider's own message says 'server-side issue, usually temporary, try again in a moment' -- and the harness treated the terminal api_error as a failed run, preserving worktrees and requiring manual reconcile-reopen-relaunch. Usage limits get recorded deadlines, bounded waits, and polling; a transient server overload, the most retryable condition there is, gets nothing.

Runs run-ff3c59bff086d6ac16dbf5101778843d and run-19dc9dff153e1eb89a2470f78f02f240.
design: Fold it into the same waiting machinery rather than inventing a third: a terminal result recognizably reporting server overload is a waitable condition with no reset time -- short interval (a minute or two, configurable), bounded by the same aggregate pause budget, each attempt recorded. This is also provider dialect: note the 529 shape on ifd.32 so the plugin contract names transient-server-refusal as one of its answers.
acceptance_criteria: A run whose provider invocation ends in a recognizable transient overload waits briefly and reissues rather than failing; the wait spends the aggregate pause budget and is recorded; repeated overloads walk into the budget rather than looping; the 529 evidence is noted on ifd.32.

title: Let the operator release a recorded usage-limit wait early
description:
A run paused on a usage limit sleeps until the provider-reported reset, and a restart deliberately honors the recorded deadline rather than re-asking -- that rule keeps a crash from retrying into a closed window. What it cannot express is the ground truth changing mid-wait: on 2026-08-18 the operator raised the account's capacity while two runs slept against an 18:50 deadline and said it should be unblocked now, and there was no verb for that.

The deadline is a fact about the provider, and the operator can change that fact. Waiting out a limit the operator has already lifted is autonomy working against its owner.
design:
An explicit operator verb, not a loosened rule: yoyo resume <item> or similar clears the recorded deadline and reissues the attempt immediately. The wait rule stays exactly as strict for everything that is not this verb. If the provider still refuses, the run re-records the new report and parks again -- the worst case of a wrong release is one refused request. Paused-seconds accounting keeps what was actually spent.

EXPANDED by operator decision, 2026-08-18: do not only add the release verb -- change the wait itself. A recorded deadline becomes an upper bound rather than a gate: the run sleeps min(probe interval, time to deadline) and then reissues the attempt, where the reissue is the probe -- a still-closed window costs one refused request and re-parks with whatever the provider now reports. The probe interval is the existing usage_limit_unknown_reset_pause (default thirty minutes), unifying the known-deadline and unknown-deadline cases into one polling discipline; the operator explicitly wants at least a thirty-minute check even under a multi-hour quoted reset, because deadlines are claims about the provider and claims go stale in both directions -- capacity gets bought mid-wait, and rolling windows can free room before the quoted edge. The release verb remains for the zero-minute case and becomes trivial: it moves the next probe to now.

Lesson from the manual release that motivated this: SIGTERM lands as a terminal cancelled run whose item stays claimed, so killing is not releasing -- recovery needed reconcile plus reopening the items and re-developing from scratch. The verb must wake the waiting process (or adjust its durable next-probe), never terminate it.
acceptance_criteria: An operator command wakes a run paused on a usage limit and reissues its attempt immediately; nothing else bypasses a recorded deadline; a release into a still-closed window re-parks cleanly; paused-time accounting survives; documented beside the behavior it overrides; a run waiting on a known reset probes at the configured interval beneath the deadline, and a probe into a still-closed window re-parks cleanly with the provider's current report; the known and unknown reset cases share one polling discipline.
notes:
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 36.

Reason: This is the goal's override clause made real: an explicit operator verb for recovery when the ground truth a run is waiting on has changed, outside the normal loop and bypassing nothing else. The item's own framing - waiting out a limit the operator has already lifted is autonomy working against its owner - is the autonomy goal read from the operator's side. The wait rule stays strict for everything that is not this verb, so the override is added without weakening what it overrides. Attributed outside the main audit pass because the item postdates it.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Serialize promotions per target branch with a store lease
description:
Settled with the operator 2026-08-18 as the concurrency invariant: development is parallel, integration is serial. At most one promotion per target branch at a time, enforced by a lease in the runstate store acquired by the promoting run's own harness -- never by an agent, and never a new daemon. The store already owns exactly this kind of cross-process coordination in Store.Reserve and the conversation lease.

This turns integration contention from a race every concurrent run can lose into an ordered queue, and reduces the yoyodyne-ifd.3.1 retry to the rare case where drift happened during the queue wait itself.
design:
A lease per product and target branch, sibling to the reservation lock: flock-style so the kernel releases it when the holder dies, acquired blocking with a bounded wait when a run reaches its promotion phase, released once the promotion settles. A crashed holder leaves no stale lock and reconcile settles its half-finished promotion, which ifd.2.8 and ifd.14 already handle.

The invariant is recorded by the architect's mechanism, not only implemented: use yoyo invariant to record 'at most one promotion per target branch, enforced by a store lease acquired by the promoting run's harness; no agent performs promotion' so it reaches developer and reviewer context per ifd.17. Ownership of the judgment stays where the design puts it: contention residue that survives the bounded retry routes to the development manager, the operator standing in until ifd.4.
acceptance_criteria: Two runs promoting into one target branch serialize through the lease; the lease dies with its process and a crashed promotion is settled by reconcile; no agent path can touch the lease or perform a promotion; the invariant is recorded via yoyo invariant and appears in developer and reviewer context; a test drives two concurrent promotions and asserts exactly one at a time with both eventually landing.
notes:
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 26.

Reason: The promotion lease is what keeps automatic integration true under concurrency: development parallel, integration serial, enforced in the store rather than by agent behavior. It turns the contention race into an ordered queue so isolated work still lands automatically when two runs finish together.

Goal served: Isolate implementation tasks in harness-managed Git worktrees and integrate successful work automatically.

title: Have the product manager open by asking about goals when there are none to read
description:
On a fresh repository the product manager opens blind: no brief, no goals, spec warnings, and nothing tells the operator that the emptiness is the point. The operator's instruction, 2026-08-18: the product manager should notice missing or minimal goals and raise it -- the first conversation on a new project should begin with the product manager asking what the product is for and offering to draft the brief and goals from the answers.

This turns the blind-repository case from a confusing silence into the intended first move. The flow it leads into is already validated: this repository's own brief was drafted by the product manager from the operator's answers and put on disk by the operator's pen.
design:
Detection belongs to the briefing, judgment to the persona. The briefing already knows whether the specifications directory has a brief and goals and whether they are stubs; say so to the product manager in so many words rather than leaving it to infer from absence. The persona then owns the move: when intent is missing or thin, open by saying what is missing, ask the questions whose answers only the operator has -- what this is, who it is for, what finished means -- and offer to draft. Minimal is a judgment call and should stay one: a two-line goals file on a young project is not a defect to nag about twice.

Do not manufacture urgency or block anything: it is an opening question, not a gate, and an operator who says later means later. The prompt addition is guidance in the persona, overridable per project like the rest of it.
acceptance_criteria: Opening a conversation on a repository with no brief or goals produces a first reply that names what is missing, asks the operator the questions a brief needs, and offers to draft; a repository with substantive goals gets no such prompt; the behavior lives in the briefing signal plus persona guidance and a project can override it; nothing is blocked or created by the prompt itself.

title: Make Yoyodyne installable: fetchable module path and a tagged release
description:
There is no way to obtain Yoyodyne except cloning this repository. go.mod names the module 'yoyodyne' rather than its repository path, so go install github.com/mason-bryant/yoyodyne/cmd/yoyo@latest cannot work; there are no tagged releases and no prebuilt binaries. For a product whose brief says it is for anyone with a repository and an idea, and whose goal says it works on other people's projects, the front door is missing.

Prioritized by the operator 2026-08-18 over the remaining artifact-governance children.
design:
Two halves, ordered. First the module rename: module github.com/mason-bryant/yoyodyne, with every internal import rewritten to match -- mechanical, repo-wide, and it must land alone so the diff stays reviewable as one thing. make build, make check, and the embedded bundle paths must survive it, and nothing user-facing changes except that go install now works.

Then the release: a tagged version and a GitHub release carrying prebuilt binaries for at least darwin-arm64, darwin-amd64, and linux-amd64, produced by a make target or workflow that a later release can rerun rather than a one-off. yoyo version should report the tag it was built from. The README install section then leads with go install and the release download, with clone-and-make remaining as the from-source path.

State plainly what a release does not promise yet: Linux and Windows are untested in the field, and the release notes should say so rather than imply parity with macOS.
acceptance_criteria: go install github.com/mason-bryant/yoyodyne/cmd/yoyo@latest produces a working binary; a tagged release exists with binaries for the three named platforms and repeatable packaging; yoyo version reports the release; make build and make check pass unchanged; the README leads its install section with the fetchable paths; untested platforms are stated as untested; the README's newcomer path reads as three steps in order -- install, yoyo init, then yoyo chat to establish the brief and goals with the product manager -- with everything else hanging off that spine, and the blind-repository case stated plainly: the product manager drafts, the operator puts the files on disk.

title: Seed Yoyodyne's own product and decision artifacts with identity and metadata
description:
ifd.1's description ends with Yoyodyne's own seeded product artifacts. The documents now exist: docs/product/brief.md, the ten v1 goals, the v1 non-goals, and the four records the operator is placing in the decision home - Beads as the durable workflow store, repository Markdown as the human-readable source of truth, the Claude Code and Codex backend decision, and the self-hosting milestone note. None carries an id, a status, or a machine-readable link upstream. Give each the identity and metadata the schema defines, and write down the references that today exist only as prose.

title: Enforce artifact ownership in code across the three artifact homes
description:
Ownership is settled and recorded on yoyodyne-ifd.21: the product manager owns docs/product, the architect owns docs/designs and the decision home with invariants beneath it, and the development manager owns no document. Today that boundary holds because personas say so and models have been observed honouring it. yoyodyne-ifd.17 showed what enforcement looks like instead - Store.Create, Amend, and Retire each call Authorize, and a test proves nothing lands on disk for any other role. Extend that from invariants to every governed artifact.

DONE: a role that does not own an artifact cannot write it, and the refusal is in code rather than instruction; a test proves nothing lands on disk for a role that does not own the target; the operator is never blocked by this, since the boundary is between agent roles.

CONSTRAINT: reuse yoyodyne-ifd.17's authorization model rather than adding a parallel one. The failure to design against is enforcement that lives in a persona a configuration can weaken; the design document already treats artifact ownership as an authorization boundary rather than a prompt convention.

title: Make a work item's goal resolve to a real goal, and attribute the existing backlog
description:
yoyodyne-ifd.24 requires every created work item to name the goal it serves and writes that onto the item's notes. Its own independent reviewer recorded the remaining gap in the same words: naming is enforced while membership in an approved goal set is not. A backlog audit on 2026-08-17 read all 18 open items and found only yoyodyne-ifd.43 carries an attribution at all; the other 17, including the epic, cite no goal, and the tracker's goal field cannot be rewritten after creation.

This is load-bearing rather than tidy. yoyodyne-ifd.25 removes per-item approval on the promise that traceability is enforced rather than asserted; its own design says that if work can reach the queue without demonstrably serving an approved goal, moving the gate up removes the gate. Enforcement against a backlog carrying no attributions either blocks everything or passes everything.

DONE: a goal named on a work item resolves to a goal artifact that exists, and one that does not is refused or reported rather than accepted as free text; an item created before this can acquire an attribution without its goal field being rewritten; the existing backlog is attributed; a legacy item with no attribution is distinguishable from one whose attribution is wrong.

CONSTRAINT: do not make the existing backlog unrunnable. A rule that fails every item admitted before attributions existed stops all work, which is worse than the gap. Whether legacy items are backfilled, grandfathered, or flagged is a decision to make explicitly and record, not to arrive at.

description:

title: Do not lose a run because the reviewer's verdict carried an unknown field
description:
Run run-2e5102d105a1c4ad772722b30b3d2635 for yoyodyne-ifd.2.6 completed its development, passed its checks, published pull request 30, and then died decoding the review: 'decode review verdict: json: unknown field severity_note'. The reviewer returned a well-formed verdict carrying one field the schema does not name, the strict decoder rejected it wholesale, and twelve dollars of approved-in-substance work became unintegrable without a single finding ever being read.

Verdicts are model-generated. A model asked for structured output will occasionally embellish the schema, and today every embellishment costs an entire run. The strictness exists to protect the verdict contract -- an unknown decision value or a missing severity must absolutely still refuse -- but an unknown *extra* field is not a corrupted verdict, it is a verbose one.
design:
Separate what strictness protects from what it merely punishes. The named fields and their values keep exactly their current validation: decision must be approve or repair, severities must be known, required fields must be present, and Resolve keeps rejecting contradictions. What changes is unknown fields: record them in the run's event stream as evidence of reviewer drift -- they are diagnostic gold for prompt regressions -- and decode the verdict without them rather than refusing it.

Failing that layer should also not be terminal when it does happen. A verdict that genuinely cannot be decoded is a failed review invocation, not a failed development: re-ask the reviewer once, the way a declined usage-limit review is simply asked again, before the run gives up. Two malformed verdicts in a row is a real signal; one is weather.

The reviewer prompt should also state the schema is closed -- cheap, and reduces the drift at its source.
acceptance_criteria: A verdict with unknown extra fields decodes, integrates the run normally, and records the unknown fields in the event stream; unknown decision values, unknown severities, missing required fields, and contradictory verdicts are still refused exactly as today; a verdict that cannot be decoded at all causes one reviewer re-ask before the run fails; the reviewer prompt states the schema is closed; a test replays the exact severity_note verdict shape from run-2e5102d105a1c4ad772722b30b3d2635 and the run survives it.

title: Rewrite the README to lead with value and match what exists
description:
The README has grown by accretion: each landed item patched its own section, so the file now reads as a pile of mechanics in landing order -- quick start, run internals, usage limits, recovery, then the conversation almost as an afterthought. The operator wants it to reasonably reflect the current state and lead with the value.

The value, as the product now actually works: an operator states intent in a conversation with a product manager that reads the product's own brief and goals, approves proposed work in batches, and watches the harness implement it in an isolated worktree, check it deterministically, review it independently, repair it when the reviewer objects, and publish it through a pull request that merges itself when CI passes -- with every gate enforced by the harness rather than by convention. The conversation is the product; yoyo run and yoyo reconcile are administrative entry points, which the design document has said for some time while the README still leads with them.

Amended by the operator, 2026-08-17: the README must also let someone else set this up and use it on their own project. Today it cannot -- the quick start assumes an initialized Yoyodyne checkout, and nowhere says how to obtain the binary, prepare a fresh repository, or adopt the harness in a project that is not Yoyodyne itself.
design:
Lead with what an operator gets, then how to get started, then how it works. A reasonable shape: what Yoyodyne does for you in a few sentences with the conversation front and center; the quick start; the conversation as the primary interface including proposals, batch decisions, /status, /work, /show, /diff, /refresh and freshness; how work flows once approved -- worktree, checks, independent review, repair loop, publication and auto-merge; configuration with the explicit file and personas; operations and recovery, including usage limits and reconcile; then pointers to the design document and configuration guide.

The discipline matters more than the structure: this repository has already shipped a README that asserted something false about the product, it surfaced as the product manager confidently reporting it to the operator as fact, and ifd.11 exists because of it. The product manager reads this file as evidence, so every sentence must be true of the current build -- lead with value, never ahead of reality. Where a capability is real but bounded (one run at a time, no scheduler, no development manager yet), say the bound in the same breath rather than leaving the reader to infer more than exists.

Preserve the hard-won operational sections rather than flattening them: what a resumed conversation knows, the usage-limit behavior including the unknown-reset poll, reconcile's guarantees, and the checks-shape guidance stay, reorganized rather than rewritten away.

The adoption path is its own section and it is written for a stranger's repository, not this one: install the prerequisites (Go for building, git, the beads CLI, the Claude Code CLI authenticated, gh authenticated if publishing), obtain and build the binary, initialize beads in the project, run yoyo init to write the explicit configuration and personas, replace the placeholder checks with the project's own commands (the configuration guide's per-language examples exist for exactly this), validate, file a first work item, and drive it from the conversation. Say which steps are optional and what each unlocks: publishing wants a remote, gh, and approvals.publishing; branch protection wants auto-merge enabled on the repository.

Verify it rather than asserting it: walk the documented steps in a scratch repository that is not Yoyodyne and fix what breaks or misleads. The language-agnostic claim says the project need not be Go, so prefer a non-Go scratch project -- this overlaps deliberately with what ifd.10 will test and the walkthrough may reuse its fixture.
acceptance_criteria: The README opens with what the product does for an operator, with the conversation as the primary interface and run/reconcile positioned as administrative; every claim is true of the current build and bounded capabilities state their bounds; the existing operational content -- resumed-conversation semantics, usage limits, recovery, configuration -- survives reorganized; the quick start still works verbatim; nothing in the file contradicts docs/configuration.md, docs/v1-harness-design.md, or the documents under docs/product/; a newcomer section documents installing Yoyodyne and adopting it in a repository that is not this one, from prerequisites through a first work item driven from the conversation, with optional steps (publishing, protection) marked as such and what they require; the documented path has actually been walked in a scratch project and works as written.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-17: 'the readme should be updated with the work that we've done. It should reasonably reflect the current state of things, lead with the value.'

title: Make proposals decidable in batches, and let the operator read items and diffs in-chat
description:
Proposals are decided one at a time: each is printed and the operator answers y or yes serially, which will grate the first time the product manager proposes five things at once. And two things the operator regularly wants mid-conversation still require leaving it: reading a work item in full (bd show) and seeing what a run actually changed (GitHub or git).

Three parts. First, render proposals as visually distinct numbered cards, using the theme. Second, batch decisions: approve 1,3 and decline 2 <reason> act on several at once, with the existing per-item semantics unchanged underneath -- approval is still recorded before creation, a decline still keeps its reason, an unanswered proposal is still named when the conversation ends. Third, /show <id> prints a work item in full, and /diff [id] shows what the conversation's running or last-finished run changed, from the durable run record.
design:
Batching changes the prompt, not the contract: the fail-closed rule from ifd.4.5 holds exactly -- nothing is created without an explicit approval naming it, an ambiguous answer declines, and each decision is recorded individually. A batch approval is several approvals, not a new kind.

/show reads through the same tracker capability the product manager already has, so what the operator sees is what the agent could see. /diff reads the durable run state and the recorded change summary rather than shelling out to git against a worktree that may already be gone; a run whose worktree was cleaned up still has its diff stat and pull request to point at.

Cards are presentation: the theme's discipline applies, and the recorded proposal payload is untouched.

title: Tell the operator how fresh the conversation's picture is, and let them refresh it
description:
The sharpest conversational failure observed so far is staleness reported as fact: twice on 2026-08-16 the product manager confidently described the repository as it was when the conversation opened, not as it stood -- once insisting documentation still said yoyodyne after it had been renamed. The mechanism is documented (the briefing is gathered once and sent on the first turn only) and the README explains when to use --new, but the operator has to remember all of that. The conversation itself never says how old its picture is.

Three parts. First, on open and resume, say when the briefing was gathered and what has moved since: 'context gathered 2h ago; 14 commits and 3 tracker changes since'. Second, a /refresh command that re-reads the repository and tracker into the running conversation without discarding it, which --new cannot do. Third, render the product manager's markdown instead of printing it raw, and colour-code /status output with the states coloured consistently: running blue, blocked orange, done green, failed red.
design:
Freshness is a comparison, not a timestamp: the briefing already records when it was assembled, and the repository and tracker can say cheaply what has changed since -- commit count from git, tracker changes from the interactions log. Print it where the operator cannot miss it, on open and after resuming, and keep it to one line.

/refresh sends the delta into the conversation as evidence, the way harness activity notices already travel: it must not silently replace what the product manager believes, it tells it what changed and lets the next reply reconcile. State plainly in the transcript that a refresh happened. A conversation that was refreshed and one that was opened fresh should end up equally current but keep different histories, and that difference is the point of the command.

Markdown rendering is presentation only, in the console layer beside the existing theme: bold, headings, lists, and rules, degrading to plain text when output is not a terminal, never touching the recorded reply. Reuse the theme's colour discipline from ifd.28: colour is an addition, every distinction survives stripping, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb are honoured.
acceptance_criteria: Opening or resuming a conversation states when its context was gathered and what has changed since; /refresh brings the running conversation current without discarding it and the transcript says it happened; the product manager's replies render markdown in a terminal and plain text elsewhere; /status output is aligned and colour-coded with the same state colours used elsewhere; the recorded conversation and --json output are unchanged by any of it.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: general request for the conversation to be easier to understand and more enjoyable. This item is the trust half: the operator should never have to wonder whether the product manager's picture is current.

title: Ship an explicit project configuration instead of inheriting hidden defaults
description:
A project configuration currently says almost nothing and inherits the rest. .yoyodyne/config.yaml carries thirteen meaningful lines and one extends: builtin:v1, while the five agents, their backends, model selectors, instance counts, and personas are supplied invisibly by a bundle inside the executable. The operator's judgement, 2026-08-16: this is difficult to reason about and more machinery than the problem needs.

The size argument for inheritance does not survive measurement. The fully expanded configuration is seventy-nine lines, and the five bundled personas are one hundred and seventy lines between them. That is roughly two hundred and fifty lines of things an operator might legitimately want to change, which is a file, not a burden.

What replaces it is a project that owns its configuration outright: every agent, selector, and persona written down where it can be read and edited, with nothing arriving from somewhere the reader cannot see.
design:
Generate rather than hand-write. yoyo init is already named in the design document's CLI surface and is the natural place: it writes a complete .yoyodyne/config.yaml with every agent stated explicitly, and copies the personas into .yoyodyne/personas/ so their text is editable in the project too. The embedded bundle survives as the template init writes from rather than as a runtime inheritance mechanism.

The cost of this is real and should be recorded rather than discovered: a project that owns its defaults stops receiving improvements to them. Better persona wording or a corrected model selector in a later Yoyodyne reaches a project only if someone re-runs init and merges the difference. Inheritance bought that and this trades it away deliberately, which is the right trade for a single-operator tool whose operator reads the file, and the wrong one for a fleet.

Keep the layering. The operator settled this on 2026-08-16: a portable configuration system is still wanted, just not yet, so extends survives as a capability while the explicit file becomes the shape a project is shipped with. Do not delete the inheritance code in internal/config or the rules tightened around it; this changes the default experience, not what the harness can express.

That means the deliverable is narrower than a rewrite. Nothing about resolution has to change. What changes is what init writes, what this repository's own configuration looks like, and what the documentation presents as the ordinary shape.

Whatever is chosen, this repository's own configuration should be migrated as part of the work, so the product is used the way it is shipped.
acceptance_criteria: yoyo init writes a complete project configuration with every agent, backend, model selector, instance count, and persona stated explicitly, and copies the persona files into the project; a project configured that way loads with no reference to a built-in bundle; extends still works for a project that uses it, and the inheritance code is retained rather than removed; this repository's own .yoyodyne/config.yaml is migrated to the explicit form; the documentation describes the explicit file as the shipped shape, and states plainly that a project owning its defaults no longer receives later improvements to them.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: 'the config file has everything commented out so that the defaults are used. I'm finding this difficult to reason about and probably a bit more complicated than we need. Replace all the defaults with explicit configurations in .yoyodyne. End users can just modify it as they see fit for their own projects.'

This reverses the direction of ifd.4.2, which introduced the bundle so a project could record only what was genuinely its own. That reasoning was about portability, and an explicit file is equally portable -- it travels with the project and needs no Yoyodyne checkout. What it gives up is shared improvement, not portability. 

Operator clarification, 2026-08-16: 'we will want those later. But at this stage of the project, I will be modifying agent properties regularly. I want those changes to be clear and obvious. That is to say, the design for a more portable agent configuration system remains a TODO.'

So this is a staging decision rather than an architectural reversal. Explicit configuration is what a project gets now, because the operator edits agent properties often and wants the effect of an edit obvious. Inheritance stays in the code and remains the answer for portability later, tracked as ifd.36. ifd.4.3 therefore stays relevant: the bundle continues to exist as the template init writes from.

title: Merge through the forge instead of pushing the target branch
description:
Publishing merges by pushing the integrated commit straight to the remote target branch and then waiting for the forge to report the pull request merged (internal/orchestrator/publish.go, 'push the integrated target branch', then awaitMerge). It never asks the forge to merge.

That works only on an unprotected branch. A repository that requires a pull request before merging -- which is the ordinary reason to open pull requests at all -- refuses the push, so the harness cannot complete the promotion it just earned. The operator wants main protected against direct pushes, and this is what stands in the way.

It also means the pull request is closed as a side effect of its commits appearing on the base, rather than merged deliberately. The forge's own record of who merged it, and by what method, is whatever it infers.
design:
Ask the forge to merge the pull request, and treat its answer as the outcome. The reviewer's approving verdict is still what authorizes it and the harness is still what acts, so the ownership rule is unchanged; only the mechanism moves from a push to a merge call.

Everything that gates integration today must still gate it: passing checks, an approving verdict, distinct developer and reviewer sessions, and a target that has not drifted. A forge merge is not an excuse to stop checking drift -- the remote can move between the check and the call, and the merge must fail rather than resolve a conflict the harness never saw.

Keep the local target branch authoritative, as ifd.29 decided. The local fast-forward still happens; what changes is that the remote arrives at the same commit through the forge rather than through a push. Decide what happens when the two disagree -- a forge that merged while the local branch did not advance is a state worth reporting rather than reconciling silently.

Choose the merge method deliberately and record it, because it decides what the history looks like: a merge commit, a squash, or a rebase produce different remote histories, and only one of them leaves the remote commit equal to the local one.

Report a refusal as what it is. A protected branch declining the merge because a required check has not run is not a harness failure, and the operator should be told which requirement was unmet.
acceptance_criteria: An approving verdict causes the harness to merge the pull request through the forge rather than by pushing the target branch; a protected branch that requires pull requests can be merged into successfully; checks, verdict, session independence, and target drift still gate the merge; the merge method is explicit and the resulting relationship between the local and remote target is defined; a forge refusal names the unmet requirement rather than being reported as a generic failure; a repository with no remote or with publishing disabled behaves exactly as it does today.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, when asked how to sequence branch protection: fix the merge path first, then enable protection requiring pull requests, requiring the build check, and including administrators. Blocks that protection work.

title: Recheck instead of blocking when a usage limit names no reset time
description:
yoyodyne-ifd.12 made a limit with no reset time stop the run and record a blocker, on the reasoning that a wait the harness cannot time is a guess. That was wrong about what the message means.

The operator's correction, 2026-08-16: the monthly spend message is misleading. It reports that the overage spend allowance is consumed, not that work is over. The ordinary five-hour window still resets on its usual schedule, so the run is waitable -- it simply has no reset time attached, because the value that was exhausted is not the one that governs when work resumes.

The captured payloads show the shape. A rejection carries overageStatus rejected with overageDisabledReason org_level_disabled, meaning there is no spillover capacity, while the five-hour window continues rolling: run-5b3b64b064f84f5d1c2da6bf620e6b1a shows resetsAt 1786912800 through the rejection and then 1786930800 once the window rolled, exactly eighteen thousand seconds later.

So the correct behavior when no reset time is given is to wait a bounded interval and ask again, not to give up. The operator's instruction is thirty minutes.
design:
Treat an absent reset time as unknown rather than as absent capacity. The run waits a default interval, thirty minutes, and reattempts; a reattempt that is refused again waits again. This replaces the blocker for that case only -- a reset time that is present but unparseable or in the past is still a malformed report and should not be trusted into a guessed wait.

The existing total bound is what keeps this safe and must apply to the polled case: execution.usage_limit_max_pause already bounds what one run may spend waiting in aggregate, so an account that keeps refusing walks into that bound rather than polling forever. Make the interval configurable rather than fixing thirty minutes in code.

Record each attempt so the operator can see a run is polling rather than stalled, and so the total spent waiting stays accurate.

Correct the documentation as part of this: README.md currently states that a limit with no reset time stops the run and records a blocker.
acceptance_criteria: A usage limit reported without a reset time causes the run to wait a configurable interval, defaulting to thirty minutes, and reattempt, rather than recording a blocker; repeated refusals continue to wait and reattempt; the aggregate pause bound still applies and stops a run that exceeds it; a reset time that is present but unparseable or already past is still refused rather than guessed; each wait and reattempt is recorded; README.md no longer says a missing reset time blocks the run.
notes: From the operator, 2026-08-16, correcting the reading in ifd.12: 'the monthly spend cap message is misleading. It just means that the cap for spend on overages is consumed, the regular 5 hour window cap will still reset on the same schedule. But since it doesn't return a resetsAt value, we should check again every 30 minutes.'
close_reason: Fixed by the operator's agent and merged through pull request 8: a usage limit reported without a reset time now waits execution.usage_limit_unknown_reset_pause and reattempts, rather than stopping the run. A reset present but not in the future is still refused.

title: Detect a stalled provider instead of killing a working one on a wall clock
description:
A provider run is bounded by a flat thirty-minute wall clock: internal/backend/claudecode sets defaultTimeout and internal/execution wraps the process in a context.WithTimeout, so context.DeadlineExceeded becomes ProcessTimedOut. Nothing asks whether the process is still working. There is no idle, liveness, or activity check anywhere in internal/execution or the Claude Code backend.

The harness already has the signal it is not using. It parses a normalized event stream and stamps every event with a time and sequence, so it knows exactly when the last one arrived. A developer that emitted a tool result seconds ago is demonstrably not hung, whatever the elapsed total.

Observed on run-a16b7d20fc58fbb52350ca37b55a4f0b for yoyodyne-ifd.22. Events run from 19:09:04 to 19:39:03, and the final three are a Bash tool call completing without error followed by thinking tokens. It was mid-work and was killed at the wall clock. The whole run was lost: 259 insertions and a new file, nothing integrable, the full cost spent. The failure is also reported as 'developer reported failure: timed_out', which is misleading -- the developer reported nothing, the harness stopped it.
design:
Separate the two questions the single timeout is currently conflating. Whether a run is stalled is answered by activity: no events for some interval means nothing is happening, and that interval can be far shorter than thirty minutes because a working agent emits events continuously. Whether a run is worth continuing is a different question, answered by a total budget, because an agent can be live and unproductive -- retrying, looping, thrashing -- and liveness alone will never catch that. Keep both, but stop using the second to answer the first.

Losing everything is the larger defect and is worth fixing even if the thresholds stay as they are. The harness already resumes provider sessions and already returns work to the same developer inside its repair loop. A run stopped for time is closer to one paused for a usage limit than to one that failed: the worktree, branch, claimed item, and session are all still good. Ending it as resumable, rather than failed, would have cost this attempt a continuation instead of a re-run.

Consider asking before killing. A developer told its remaining time is short can finish what it is holding and summarize; a developer killed mid-edit cannot. That is only worth doing if the harness can tell a wrap-up from a stall, which is the same activity signal.

Scope the change to provider runs. The same Timeout field bounds short git commands where a flat deadline is exactly right.
acceptance_criteria: A provider run that is still emitting events is not stopped for elapsed time alone; a run that stops emitting events is detected within an interval much shorter than the current total timeout; a total budget still bounds a live but unproductive run; a run stopped for either reason preserves its worktree, branch, claimed item, and session and is reported as resumable rather than failed where the work is still good; the reported reason distinguishes a stall from an exhausted budget, and neither is described as the developer having reported a failure; git commands keep their existing flat deadlines.
notes:
Raised by the operator, 2026-08-16: 'Why would the harness kill it? Shouldn't it just check to see if the process is still going?' The answer is that it should, and it already has the event stream to do it with.

title: Publish work through pull requests, opened by the developer step and merged by the reviewer's verdict
description:
Integration currently ends at the local target branch. Nothing in the harness pushes -- there is no git push anywhere in internal/ -- and nothing opens a pull request, so main accumulates work that is invisible until the operator pushes by hand. The design document does not cover this at all: it describes a local, single-operator harness and the words push, remote branch, and pull request do not appear in it.

The operator's direction, 2026-08-16: the harness should open pull requests; the developer step is responsible for opening and pushing them; the reviewer merges them once satisfied.
design:
The harness performs, the roles decide. This is the existing rule rather than a new one -- the ownership table already gives workflow state, worktrees, checks, and integration to the harness, with agents able to request actions but not bypass policy, and the design states agents do not create, assign, merge, or remove their own worktrees. Applying it here: the developer's phase is what causes a branch to be pushed and a pull request opened, and the reviewer's approving verdict is what causes the merge, but the harness executes both. No agent is handed a credential or a shell to run gh with.

That distinction is the safety property and must not be implemented away. A reviewer agent that could merge is a reviewer that can be talked into merging; a reviewer whose verdict the harness acts on cannot bypass the checks, the independence evidence, or the fast-forward rule that already gate integration. Everything that gates integration today gates the merge.

Decide what merging means for the local target branch. Today integration fast-forwards main directly; if a pull request is the unit of promotion, the local branch either follows the merge or stops being the thing that moves, and having both would give a project two answers about where its work is.

Publishing has a wider blast radius than moving a local branch, so it belongs under approvals beside integration rather than being unconditional: a project should opt into pushing the way it opts into automatic integration, and a repository with no remote configured must degrade to today's local behavior rather than failing.

The design document's Git model needs extending as part of this, not after it.
acceptance_criteria: A run pushes its branch and opens a pull request as part of the developer phase, performed by the harness rather than by an agent; an approving reviewer verdict causes the harness to merge it, subject to the same checks, independence evidence, and fast-forward rule that gate integration today; no agent has credentials, shell access, or the ability to merge directly; the relationship between a merged pull request and the local target branch is defined and only one of them is authoritative; publishing is configurable under approvals and a repository with no remote still works as it does today; the design document's Git model covers remotes and pull requests.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: 'Harness should open PRs. Devs should be responsible for opening and pushing them. Reviewers should merge them, after they're satisfied.'

Reading recorded explicitly, since the instruction can be read two ways: the developer and reviewer phases are what trigger publishing and merging, and the harness is what carries them out. The alternative -- agents invoking gh themselves -- would hand a credential to an agent reading untrusted repository content and would let a reviewer merge without the harness enforcing its verdict. If that reading is wrong, this needs revisiting before it is built. Relates to ifd.2.6, branch-scope review, which becomes more useful once there is a pull request to review against.
