The harness pushes the run branch and the integrated commit to the configured remote (`Manager.pushBranch` uses `m.remote`), but `gh pr list` and `gh pr create` are run with only `Dir` set, so `gh` resolves the target repository by its own remote heuristics (it prefers a remote named `upstream`, then `github`, then `origin`, and errors asking for `gh repo set-default` when several GitHub remotes exist). docs/configuration.md tells a project `remote: origin   # the default; name another remote if yours is not origin`, and internal/config/inheritance_test.go exercises `remote: upstream`, so a repository with more than one remote can have its branch pushed to one repository while the pull request is opened against — or queried in — another, or can fail at `Ensure` after the branch is already published. Wire the configured remote through to the publisher (resolve it once via `git remote get-url <remote>` and pass `--repo`/`GH_REPO` on every `gh` call), and cover it with a test that a non-`origin` `execution.remote` reaches the forge commands.
Finding [minor] (docs/v1-harness-design.md:312): The acceptance criterion asks that no agent have credentials or the ability to merge directly. The reviewer side is genuinely enforced (no tools), but the developer side is only documented as unenforced and deferred, in docs/v1-harness-design.md ("Not enforced for the developer") and docs/configuration.md. The documentation is accurate and the deferral is defensible, but nothing in the evidence records a tracked follow-up for withholding or scrubbing forge credentials from the developer process, so the gap has no owner. File it as a work item, or state the deferral where it will be picked up rather than only in prose.

title: Show a conversation working, and separate who said what with colour
description:
An interactive turn prints nothing between the operator's message and the reply, so a turn that takes a minute is indistinguishable from a hang. The operator hit this on 2026-08-16 and reasonably concluded the command was broken. It was not: conversation chat-2d493303331a06ef746e1ace4a942068 records the turn opening, seven consecutive provider rejections with exponential backoff over about thirty-six seconds (system api_retry, error unknown, max_retries 10), and only then the model generating. Every one of those events was recorded and none reached the operator. The harness already knows what is happening; this is a reporting gap.

The transcript should also make it obvious at a glance who is speaking and where one exchange ends and the next begins.

Split from yoyodyne-ifd.22, which now covers input separation alone after carrying all three concerns exceeded a run's timeout.
design:
Show that work is in progress and say something about what kind, without turning the terminal into an event log. A spinner or equivalent answers 'is it alive'; a short phrase for the phase answers 'what is it doing'. The event stream already carries the phases worth naming: the turn starting, provider retries, the model generating, and a tool or command running.

Provider retries deserve to be named rather than folded into generic waiting. A turn that is slow because the provider is refusing requests is telling the operator something about their account or the service, and it is the case most likely to look like a hang.

Do not let the indicator hide a real stall: an activity display that animates while nothing is happening is worse than silence, because it looks like progress.

Separate the operator's turn from the reply with a horizontal rule, and use colour to distinguish kinds of thing rather than to decorate. A question the product manager asks the operator should stand out, in orange, because a question that scrolls past unanswered stalls the work; proposals awaiting a decision and the harness's own command output are the other kinds worth distinguishing, since both are things the operator must act on rather than read.

Colour is an addition to the text, never the carrier of meaning: every distinction made with colour must survive being stripped. Honour NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb, suppress colour and rules when output is not a terminal, and keep both out of --json. The recorded event stream and reply text stay exactly as they are.
acceptance_criteria: An interactive turn shows continuous evidence of activity from the operator's message until the reply; the display names what is happening at least coarsely and names provider retries specifically; a turn with no provider activity for an extended period is distinguishable from one progressing; a horizontal rule separates the operator's turn from the reply; questions the product manager asks, proposals awaiting decision, and harness command output are visually distinguished, questions in orange; every distinction survives colour being stripped; NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, and non-terminal output suppress colour and rules; none of it contaminates the recorded reply, the event stream, or --json.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, in two parts: chats should provide a status indicator such as a spinner and feedback about what it is doing, so it is clear something is happening; and use colour, with questions in orange, and a horizontal rule between the operator's turn and the reply. Depends on ifd.22: an indicator that animates into the line the operator is typing makes the original complaint worse.

title: Give the product manager real authority over the tracker
description:
The product manager owns product intent but cannot act on the tracker or see enough of it to reason. Both limits are deliberate and both are wrong as they stand.

It has no tools at all: internal/chat sets AllowedTools to empty with permission mode plan, so every tracker change is dictated to the operator to type. Asked to remove a dependency, it answers that the edit is theirs. The reasoning for toollessness was that the product manager reads untrusted repository content while talking directly to the operator, so filesystem and command access is an injection surface. That holds for shell and filesystem. It does not justify blocking structured tracker operations, and conflating 'no arbitrary tools' with 'no authority' is the mistake.

It also sees very little. The briefing lists open items as titles only, capped at fifteen per group and one hundred and twenty bytes each (maxSurveyItems, maxSurveyTitleBytes in internal/chat/work.go). It cannot read a description, so it cannot tell whether proposed work belongs inside an existing item or beside it, and says so rather than guessing. Asking it to own a backlog while showing it truncated titles is asking for judgement without evidence.
design:
Grant authority through a narrow, structured tracker capability rather than by handing over general tools. Creating, updating, reparenting, reprioritising, linking and unlinking dependencies, and closing are bounded operations with named arguments that can be validated, recorded, and reversed. Shell and filesystem access remain refused, and the distinction is the point: the injection surface that argued against tools is arbitrary execution, not a typed call against the work tracker.

Goals are the exception the operator named and they stay guarded. The product manager may propose a change to a goal and may not make one, which is the existing ownership rule rather than a new restriction; what changes is that everything else stops being treated as if it were a goal.

Visibility has to match the authority. Reading an item in full is a request the product manager makes when it needs one, not a larger dump in every briefing: the survey stays a summary and detail is fetched on demand, so the context cost lands only where judgement actually requires it. The fifteen-item and one-hundred-and-twenty-byte caps are summary bounds and should stay bounds, but an item the product manager cannot read at all is worse than one it reads late.

Everything it does is recorded in the conversation and visible to the operator, and it says what it did rather than only what it decided. Treat retrieved item text as evidence, exactly as repository documents already are: a description is data describing work, never an instruction to follow.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can create, update, reparent, reprioritise, link, unlink, and close work items directly, without dictating the change to the operator; it can read any work item in full on request rather than only titles; it still cannot change a goal, and proposes one instead; it has no filesystem, command, or network access; every tracker action it takes is recorded in the conversation and reported to the operator; retrieved work-item text is treated as evidence rather than instruction; an action that fails is reported as failed rather than described as done.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, after a conversation in which the product manager dictated Beads edits and could not tell whether proposed work duplicated an existing item: 'The PM should have broad authority to see and edit beads -- it should only be very careful about editing goals.'

Supersedes the advisory-only stance from ifd.4.5, which was a deliberate first step rather than a permanent position. This should land before ifd.18 and ifd.24, which both assume a product manager that can actually manage a queue.

title: See and control work the harness is running on its own
description:
Once a development manager pulls from the product manager's queue and work runs without the operator starting each item, the operator needs to see what is happening and be able to stop it. Visibility is what makes autonomy acceptable rather than alarming: work proceeding out of sight is indistinguishable from work happening behind your back.

What exists today assumes the operator started the run. /status reports in flight, claimed, blocked, available, and done, and /stop cancels the run this conversation started and settles what it left behind. Neither was built for several items moving at once, chosen by something other than the operator, and /stop in particular is scoped to the conversation's own run.
design:
The operator should be able to answer three questions without leaving the conversation: what is running now and why it was chosen, what it is doing, and what it has changed. Why it was chosen is the one with no equivalent today and it is the one that matters when the harness picked the work rather than the operator: an item running with no visible reason is the failure this is meant to prevent.

Control has to reach further than one run. Stopping the item that is running, stopping a development manager from starting anything more, and stopping everything are different intentions and should not collapse into one verb. Pausing intake while letting current work finish is the case an operator reaches for when something looks wrong but not urgent, and it is the hardest to add later.

Stopping stays as careful as it is now: the existing stop settles what the cancelled run left behind rather than abandoning it, and that must hold when the stop was not aimed at a run the conversation started. Report what actually happened rather than what was asked for, including a run that finished before the stop reached it.
acceptance_criteria: The operator can see every item in flight, what each is doing, and why it was selected, without leaving the conversation; can stop one item, pause a development manager from starting more, and stop everything, as distinct actions; stopping settles what a cancelled run left behind exactly as it does today; the report says what happened rather than what was requested, including work that finished before the stop arrived; none of it requires the operator to have started the work.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: 'I want visibility into how the dev managers are working and the ability to stop things.' Paired with ifd.25, which removes per-item approval: that trade is only safe if the operator can see and stop what was admitted without asking.
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 25.

Reason: Seeing and stopping work the harness chose is what makes near-autonomy acceptable rather than alarming; the item's own text says work proceeding out of sight is indistinguishable from work happening behind your back, and it is paired with ifd.25 as the visibility that makes removing per-item approval safe. Inspection, recovery, and override are exactly the goal's stated exceptions to the normal loop.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Move approval from each work item up to the goals
description:
The operator should approve goals, not every work item. Approving each item is what makes the current loop require an operator for every step, and it is the thing standing between the harness and running work on its own.

This is a return to the stated design rather than a departure from it. docs/v1-harness-design.md already says the human explicitly approves the initial brief and goals, and that lower-level approval gates are configurable but disabled by default. Per-proposal approval exists because there is no development manager yet: with nothing to decompose an approved goal into work, the product manager proposes items directly and the operator is the only thing standing between a proposal and the tracker.

Once goals are approved artifacts (yoyodyne-ifd.20) and something pulls from a product-manager-owned queue (yoyodyne-ifd.18, yoyodyne-ifd.4), the gate belongs at the goal: approve what the product should do, then watch it happen.
design:
Approval moves up a level; it does not disappear. What the operator approves is a goal, and work that traces to an approved goal is admitted without a further prompt. That places the whole weight of the arrangement on traceability actually being enforced rather than asserted, which is why this depends on yoyodyne-ifd.24: if work can reach the queue without demonstrably serving an approved goal, moving the gate up removes the gate.

Some things must still stop and ask, and they are exactly the cases the product manager is meant to escalate: work that traces to no goal, work that contradicts one, and a change to the goals themselves. A goal is amended by the operator, never by work flowing through the queue.

Keep it configurable rather than replacing one fixed policy with another. approvals already carries brief, goals, designs, and integration; per-item approval should become a policy an operator can turn back on, since the level of trust that suits an established product does not suit its first week.

The operator must be able to see what was admitted without being asked. Autonomy that is invisible is indistinguishable from work happening behind your back, so this is only safe alongside the visibility yoyodyne-ifd.26 covers.
acceptance_criteria: Work that traces to an approved goal is admitted to the queue without per-item approval; work that traces to no goal, contradicts one, or would change a goal still stops and asks; per-item approval remains available as configuration; what was admitted without asking is visible to the operator after the fact; the default for a new project is stated deliberately rather than inherited by accident.
notes: Design precondition reported by ifd.1.8's reviewer: yoyo artifact approve records 'by: operator' on the strength of who ran the command, and nothing distinguishes the operator from an agent with shell access. Harmless while the approval record gates nothing — ifd.1.8's explicit constraint — but this item makes goal-level approval load-bearing, at which point a forgeable approval is an agent able to admit its own work. Decide the authentication story (or an equivalent boundary) before or as part of this item.

title: Have the product manager validate proposals against its goals and say when something smells wrong
description:
The product manager should check work against its goals before proposing it, not after, and should be willing to push back rather than only comply.

Nothing checks this today. Proposal.Validate in internal/chat/proposal.go checks shape only: a title that is present, one line, and bounded; description and rationale present; parent and dependency identifiers well-formed and not duplicated. It never asks whether the proposed work serves a goal. Identifiers are only format-checked, so a proposal can name a parent that does not exist and still validate.

What holds the line today is instruction. The persona says every piece of downstream work must trace to an active goal, and the model has been observed honouring it unprompted -- declining to parent an item under the v1 epic because the work did not trace to an active goal. That is the model being conscientious, not the harness refusing.
design:
Validation runs before the operator is asked, so what reaches them is work the product manager already believes serves a goal, with the goal it serves named. A proposal that traces to nothing is not silently dropped: the product manager says it cannot place the work and asks, because unattributable work is usually a sign the goals are incomplete rather than that the request was wrong.

Being opinionated is the substantive half and needs to survive contact with a model that wants to be agreeable. When work would violate a goal, or fits the letter while cutting against the spirit of the product, the product manager says so and asks for instructions rather than proposing it with a caveat attached. The failure to design against is a concern raised so softly it reads as assent. A concern is a question that stops and waits, not a sentence in a paragraph the operator skims.

Distinguish the cases rather than collapsing them: work that serves a goal, work that serves none, work that contradicts one, and work that is technically consistent but that the product manager judges to be against the product's intent. The last is a judgement it should be willing to make and be wrong about, because an operator can overrule a stated opinion and cannot overrule one that was never voiced.

Verify what identifiers name. A parent or dependency that does not exist should fail before the operator is asked to approve it.
acceptance_criteria: Every proposal names the goal it serves, and one that traces to no goal is raised as a question rather than proposed or dropped; a proposal that would violate a goal is not proposed, and the conflict is put to the operator as a question that waits for an answer; the product manager states an opinion when work is consistent with the goals but against the product's intent; parents and dependencies are verified to exist before the operator is asked; the distinction between these cases is visible to the operator rather than flattened into one warning.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: the product manager should validate everything it proposes against its goals before proposing them, and be opinionated -- if something seems like it might violate goals or the spirit of the product, say so and request instructions.

Operator decision, 2026-08-16: approval is moving to the goal level (ifd.25), which makes this item the thing that keeps that safe. Traceability here has to be enforced rather than asserted -- if work can reach the queue without demonstrably serving an approved goal, moving the gate up removes the gate rather than raising it.

title: Separate the conversation's input from its output
description:
What the operator is typing and what the harness is writing share one stream. internal/chat reads stdin with a line-oriented bufio.Scanner and writes with plain fmt.Fprint, so anything arriving while the operator types lands in the middle of the line they are composing, and the transcript stops showing who said what or where the conversation has got to.

This is the foundation the rest of the conversation's usability rests on, which is why it is now its own item. A first attempt (run-a16b7d20fc58fbb52350ca37b55a4f0b, preserved at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-22/a16b7d20, commit c08f40c) carried this together with an activity indicator and colour, reached 259 insertions and a new internal/chat/display.go, and hit the thirty minute provider timeout unfinished. The indicator and colour are now yoyodyne-ifd.28 and depend on this.

It also explains a workaround already shipped. A finished background run is reported only when the operator next presses enter, asks for /status, or waits for it -- deliberately, because there is no safe moment to write unprompted. Once input has its own region that deferral can be dropped and a run can report when it actually finishes.
design:
The composing line must survive anything printed above it: a reply, a proposal, a run completing. Text already typed is never lost, reordered, or mixed with output, and the operator can tell at a glance which text is theirs and which is the product manager's.

Preserve ordinary terminal expectations while doing it -- scrollback of the conversation so far, the terminal's own copy and paste, and resizing -- since a conversation the operator cannot scroll back through or copy out of is a poor trade for a tidy input line.

Degrade honestly: when output is not a terminal this is an ordinary stream of text with no cursor control, and the recorded conversation is identical either way.
acceptance_criteria: The operator's input occupies its own region that output never writes into, so text being typed is never interrupted, reordered, or lost when a reply, a proposal, or a completing run arrives; a background run reports when it finishes rather than waiting for the operator to press a key; scrollback, copy and paste, and terminal resizing continue to work; when output is not a terminal there is no cursor control and the recorded conversation is identical; none of it reaches the recorded reply, the event stream, or --json output.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, in three parts. First, after ./bin/yoyo chat --new appeared to do nothing: chats with the product manager should provide a status indicator such as a spinner and some feedback about what it is doing; it should be clear that something is happening. Second: use colour, with questions in orange, and a horizontal rule between the operator's turn and the product manager's reply. Third: split the input area from the output, as Claude Code does -- 'sometimes I'm typing something when a response comes back, it goes into the middle of my text and then it's not clear what the agent said and what I was typing or even where we are in the conversation.'

Sizing note for whoever picks this up: the third part changes how the conversation loop talks to the terminal, since internal/chat currently reads with a line-oriented bufio.Scanner and writes with plain fmt.Fprint. It is a larger change than the first two and they depend on it -- an activity indicator that animates into the line the operator is typing makes the reported problem worse. If this is split, build input separation first and treat the indicator, colour, and rules as what follows.

title: Have the product manager work from a configurable specifications directory
description:
The product manager should build its picture of product intent from specification documents in one configured directory, defaulting to docs/specs, rather than from whatever Markdown the repository happens to contain.

A specification opens with an introductory paragraph stating what the thing is and why it exists, followed by the goals that serve it. The goals must support and stay consistent with that introduction, and the product manager is responsible for keeping all work consistent with those goals.

Today internal/chat assembles the product manager's context from README.md, everything under docs/, and Beads state. That is broad and undirected: it mixes product intent with architecture and operator documentation, and it is why a stale sentence in README.md was reported to the operator as current product fact on 2026-08-16.
design:
Add the specifications path to the configuration schema with docs/specs as the default, resolved like other project paths and confined to the repository. It is a directory of specifications rather than one file, so the product manager holds several coherent units of intent rather than a single brief.

The structure is the contract: introduction first, goals after, goals consistent with the introduction. State it where it is enforceable rather than only in prose, and decide what the harness does with a specification that does not follow it -- refusing to load it silently loses intent, so it should surface rather than disappear.

Narrowing the product manager's inputs is a deliberate trade and should be made knowingly. Reading all of docs/ is what let it notice a contradiction between documentation and reality; reading only docs/specs makes it authoritative about intent and blind to everything else. Decide explicitly whether it still sees anything outside the specifications directory, and record the reasoning either way.

This substantially defines the product-artifact half of yoyodyne-ifd.1, which described artifact governance without settling what a product artifact looks like on disk.
acceptance_criteria: The specifications directory is configurable with docs/specs as the default and is confined to the repository; the product manager's context is built from specifications in that directory; a specification that does not follow the introduction-then-goals structure is surfaced rather than silently ignored; what the product manager can see outside the directory is a recorded decision rather than an accident; docs/configuration.md documents the setting.
notes:
Operator decision, 2026-08-16: the path is docs/product/, not docs/specs. The product manager proposed it during a conversation and the operator confirmed it when asked directly, before the path became configurable. ifd.20.1 built it and ifd.20.2 targets docs/product/goals/.

title: Collect agent findings and warnings for the operator
description:
Every agent type needs a way to report something important that does not stop its work, so it reaches the operator instead of being lost.

Today an agent can only reach the operator by failing. The pipeline records a blocker when a repair budget is spent (blockOnUnresolvedFindings, blockOnFailingCheck) and Beads has a human-needed flag, but both are terminal: they mean work stopped. Anything an agent notices while succeeding -- a risk it worked around, a fragile assumption, a discovery outside its scope -- survives only as prose in a run summary copied into bead notes, where nothing surfaces it. Real examples from this session that reached the operator only because a human was reading: the reviewer's observation that the built-in bundle's declared version had become inert, and a developer's report that bd lint could not run in its sandbox.

Collect these raw for now. Filtering by an agent is a later question and should not gate collection.
design:
A report is not a blocker and must not be modelled as one: work continues, and nothing about it stops or claims the operator's attention as a failure does. Keep the record structured enough to be filtered later without deciding the filter now -- reporting agent and role, run and work item, severity, and the text -- since a raw pile with no structure cannot be triaged when volume grows.

Every role reports through one mechanism, including the product manager, whose conversation is otherwise the only channel that reaches the operator at all. Surfacing belongs in the operator's normal path rather than a separate tool, which after ifd.16 means the product-manager conversation.

Volume is the risk. A channel that fills with routine observations gets ignored, and then it is worse than nothing because it looks like coverage. Guidance on what merits a report belongs in the role contracts, where it cannot be weakened by a persona.

title: Give the product manager ownership of the work backlog
description:
The product manager owns the backlog that development managers pull from. It decides what is worth doing and in what order, as the expression of product intent it already owns; a development manager takes from that ordered backlog and decomposes, sequences, and assigns the implementation work.

This makes explicit a boundary the roles already imply. The product manager owns the brief and goals but has no say today over what is actually worked on next, which means priority is set by whoever picks the next item -- currently the operator, by hand.
design:
Keep the existing ownership split rather than widening the product manager's authority into implementation. Ordering and admission to the backlog are product decisions; decomposition, dependency structure, and assignment remain the development manager's. A development manager that disagrees with an ordering proposes a change rather than reordering, exactly as downstream roles already propose changes to goals.

Priority already exists in Beads, so the question is who is authoritative for it and how that is enforced, not where to store it. Deletion is the sharp edge: removing work from a backlog can silently drop scope the operator asked for, which the product-manager persona already forbids. Retirement should be explicit and recorded, not a delete.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can admit work to the backlog and order it, and that ordering is what a development manager consumes; a role other than the product manager cannot reorder or admit work, only propose; retiring work is explicit and recorded rather than a silent removal; the ordering is visible to the operator from the product-manager conversation.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: the product manager should be responsible for managing the backlog of work that the development manager(s) pull from. Clarified the same day: this is a priority queue, and the operator does not want to start each item by hand -- 'I don't want to have to do /work ITEMID for each thing to get it going.'

That makes this the hinge of the autonomous loop rather than a bookkeeping feature. The queue is what a development manager pulls from without being told, so ordering is not advisory: it decides what happens next. Related: ifd.24 (work is validated against goals before it reaches the queue), ifd.25 (approval moves from each item up to the goals), ifd.26 (the operator can see and stop what is pulled), ifd.3 (the scheduler that actually runs it), ifd.4 (the development manager that pulls).

title: Give the architect ownership of durable architectural invariants
description:
Architectural invariants are cross-cutting constraints that must hold across work items: a contract one item established that later items must not break. They should be rare and consequential, created, amended, and retired by the architect, and they exist to stop a developer whose own work looks correct from breaking something outside its scope.

This is currently done by hand and the absence is measurable. The first yoyodyne-ifd.2.7 attempt bypassed Store.Reserve, which was the only thing preventing two processes acting on one in-flight item. The first yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 attempt added a second resume path beside the one ifd.2.7 had just built and broke its contract, discarding 474 insertions of otherwise working code. Both were caught late by a reviewer or by failing tests, and both were prevented on the retry only because the constraint was transcribed into the bead by hand.
design:
An invariant is a durable artifact the architect owns, not prose in a bead. It needs stable identity, a statement of what must hold and why, the work item or design that established it, and a lifecycle including retirement, since an invariant that no longer holds is worse than none. Ownership follows the existing model: only the architect creates or amends one, others propose.

The point of failure to design against is delivery, not authorship. An invariant nobody puts in front of the developer does not constrain anything, so invariants relevant to a work item must reach the developer's context and the reviewer's evidence without depending on whoever wrote the bead remembering. Scope selection matters: every invariant in every prompt is both expensive and ignorable.

Relates to ifd.11, which put documentation reconciliation in the developer contract and asked the reviewer to report contradicted documentation; invariants are the same delivery problem for a stricter class of claim. Relates to ifd.2.6, which catches after the fact what invariants aim to prevent up front.
acceptance_criteria: The architect can create, amend, and retire an invariant as a durable artifact with stable identity and rationale; invariants relevant to a work item reach both the developer's context and the reviewer's evidence without per-bead transcription; a change that violates a delivered invariant draws a finding; no role other than the architect can create or amend one; retirement is explicit and recorded.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: invariants should be rare but important, and exist to keep developers from doing work that breaks something cross-cutting or outside the scope of that developer's work. Gated behind ifd.16.

title: Threshold: manage work end to end through the product-manager conversation
description:
A threshold rather than a feature, in the style of the self-hosting thresholds in docs/v1-harness-design.md. It is met when the operator can run the product loop entirely by talking to the product manager: state intent, have it become approved goals and Beads work, see what is in flight and what is blocked, redirect or stop work, and answer what the product manager escalates -- without reaching for yoyodyne run or bd to make any of it happen.

Explicit-ID execution and direct bd access remain available for inspection, recovery, and override. The threshold is that they are no longer required for ordinary work.

Operator directive (2026-08-16): no work gated behind this threshold begins before it is met. The point is to avoid building more agent machinery that can only be driven by hand.
design: Compose what exists rather than adding a parallel path: yoyodyne chat (ifd.4.4) already holds a durable conversation, and ifd.4.5 gives the product manager a governed way to propose Beads work for operator approval. What remains is the operator seeing and steering work from inside that conversation rather than from a second tool.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can take a stated intent through to integrated work using only the product-manager conversation; can see in-flight, blocked, and completed work from within it; and can redirect or stop work through it. Nothing gated behind this threshold is started until that is demonstrated.

title: Return failing checks to the developer like reviewer findings
description:
The repair loop returns reviewer findings to the same developer for a bounded number of attempts, but a failing deterministic check ends the run outright. In internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go, activeRun.verify is called before review and again inside repairLoop after each repair attempt, and in both places a failure is returned as an error rather than handed back to the developer.

This is a real cost, not a theoretical asymmetry. Run run-b0414b72946f17eb3eb95acd5287b67f on yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 produced 474 insertions of working reconciliation code and was discarded because one test failed: the resume path it added broke TestPipelineResumesTheRepairLoopAtTheRecordedAttempt, an existing test encoding the repair-loop semantics from yoyodyne-ifd.2.7. A single iteration would very likely have fixed it. Instead the whole run was lost, and re-running costs roughly the same as the original attempt.

A failing check is better repair input than a reviewer finding: it is deterministic, reproducible, and names the exact failure.
design:
Treat a failed check as a repair trigger with the same shape and the same budget as a repair verdict. The developer is resumed in the same worktree with its session, given the failing command, its exit code, and its captured output, and the checks are then re-run.

Do not weaken the gate. The existing rule that review and integration are reachable only through passing checks must hold exactly as it does now; this changes how many times the developer may attempt to reach that state, not whether it is required. An approval must still belong to a change whose checks passed.

Decide and state whether check repairs and review repairs share one budget or hold separate ones. Sharing one is simpler and bounds total developer invocations, which is what the budget exists to do; separate budgets risk a run that alternates between the two and consumes far more than the operator expects. Record the attempts durably as the existing loop does, so an interrupted attempt still counts and a restart cannot buy a fresh budget.

Bound the failure output handed back so a verbose failing suite cannot dominate the developer's context.
acceptance_criteria: A failing check returns the command, exit code, and captured output to the same developer in the same worktree and re-runs the checks, up to the configured budget; review and integration remain unreachable while any check fails; the budget is enforced across both repair kinds and the chosen accounting is documented; attempts are recorded before the developer is invoked so a restart resumes at the right attempt; failure output handed to the developer is bounded; tests with a fake backend cover check-fail-then-pass, check-fail-until-budget-spent, and that a passing review cannot be reached with a failing check.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 when ifd.2.8 was discarded for one failing test. Touches the same repairLoop as ifd.2.7, so it should not run concurrently with other pipeline work.
Yoyodyne run passed checks, was approved by an independent reviewer, and was integrated automatically.

title: Pause and resume work when the provider reports a usage limit
description:
When the provider reports that a usage limit is exhausted and names a time at which it resets, the harness should wait until that time and continue, rather than treating the limit as a failure of the work.

Today it cannot even see the reset time. The Claude Code adapter's stream parser routes rate_limit_event to the outer default branch (internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go, the default in parseLine), which emits only provider_type and provider_subtype; streamEnvelope declares no field for a reset timestamp, so encoding/json discards it. Twenty rate_limit_event entries appear across recorded runs and every one has an empty payload. The transient case is already handled inside the provider CLI and surfaces as the system api_retry subtype with attempt and max_retries; this bead is about the hard case, where waiting is the only remedy.

Because the fields were discarded, the exact shape of a hard-limit envelope has never been captured. Do not infer it from documentation or from this description: capture the raw envelope first and implement against what the provider actually sends.
design:
Work in two stages, and do not skip the first. Stage one: preserve the provider's rate-limit envelope rather than reducing it to two fields, so the real payload is recorded in the event stream and can be inspected. Stage two: act on it.

Distinguish the two cases. A transient throttle is the provider CLI's business and already appears as api_retry; the harness should not duplicate that. A hard usage limit with a reset time is the harness's business, because only it knows the work is worth resuming.

On a hard limit the run must pause, not fail. Nothing is cleaned up, the Beads item stays claimed, the worktree and branch survive, and the developer session identifier is retained so work resumes in context rather than restarting. Record the reset deadline in durable run state before waiting, so a process that dies during the wait does not lose the deadline and a restart does not immediately retry into the same limit. This is the same resumability yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 builds for interrupted runs and should reuse it rather than inventing a parallel path.

Bound the wait with configuration: a maximum pause, after which the run stops and records a blocker rather than sleeping indefinitely. Treat a reset time that is absent, unparseable, or implausibly far in the future as no reset time at all and stop rather than guessing. Never busy-wait or retry before the deadline.

Open design question for the implementer to settle and state: whether a long wait should be spent in process or whether the run should exit resumable and be continued by a later invocation. Waiting in process is what the operator asked for and is simplest to reason about; an hours-long sleep in a CLI process is not. A reasonable resolution is to wait in process below a configured threshold and exit resumable above it, provided the resumable path is genuinely exercised by yoyodyne-ifd.2.8.
acceptance_criteria: A hard usage-limit report pauses the run instead of failing it, with the worktree, branch, claimed Beads item, and developer session all preserved; the reset deadline is recorded durably before the wait begins and is honored across a process restart; work resumes automatically once the deadline passes and completes normally; a missing, unparseable, or implausible reset time stops the run with a blocker rather than a guessed wait; the configured maximum pause is enforced; a transient api_retry is not mistaken for a hard limit; the provider's rate-limit payload is preserved in the event stream rather than reduced to its type; tests with a fake backend cover pause-then-resume, restart during the wait, and the refusal cases.
notes:
Raised by the operator 2026-08-16 after observing that runs stop when tokens run out. Depends on yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 because both persist and resume interrupted run state, and building them independently would produce two resume paths.

title: Reconcile documentation as part of definition of done
description:
Every gate in the harness is diff-scoped: checks run commands against one change, and the reviewer judges one change against its work item. Nothing compares a documented claim to reality, so a change that falsifies existing documentation integrates cleanly and the documentation stays wrong.

This is not hypothetical. README.md line 38 asserted that the harness 'does not yet commit, integrate, or close the item automatically' from the moment yoyodyne-ifd.2.4 shipped automatic integration until 2026-08-16. The reviewer that approved ifd.2.4 never saw it, because README was not in that diff. It surfaced only when the product manager, whose only evidence is repository documents and Beads state, faithfully reported the stale claim as current fact to the operator.

That failure mode matters more now than it would have before: the product manager is the operator's routine interface and has no tools with which to verify anything it reads, so a false document becomes a false answer with full confidence.
design:
Two complementary parts, in order of cost.

First, make the reviewer ask whether the change falsifies anything documented. The reviewer already receives the work item, the diff, and the check results; the addition is an explicit instruction to identify documentation the change contradicts, and a finding when it does. This catches drift at the moment it is created, which is the only cheap moment. Its limit is real and should be stated rather than papered over: the reviewer sees a diff, not the whole corpus, so it will catch a change that contradicts documentation it can see and will miss one that invalidates a claim in a file the change never touches.

Second, define done for a work item as including the documentation that describes the behavior it changes. This belongs in the developer contract rather than in each bead, so it applies without every author remembering it.

Deliberately out of scope: giving the product manager tools to verify claims itself. It is toolless on purpose -- it cannot be induced to act by anything in the untrusted documents it reads -- and granting filesystem or command access to the one agent in direct conversation with the operator trades a documentation problem for a prompt-injection surface. Fix the documents instead.

The deeper blind spot, that properties of the accumulated whole are invisible from any single diff, is shared with yoyodyne-ifd.2.6 and is not fully solved here.
acceptance_criteria: The reviewer identifies and reports documentation a change contradicts, and a change that falsifies a visible documented claim draws a finding; the developer contract states that documentation describing changed behavior is part of the work; a test demonstrates the reviewer flagging a diff that contradicts documentation included in its evidence; the known limit, that claims in untouched files are not covered, is recorded rather than implied.

title: Add the two-attempt developer repair loop
description:
Milestone 1 of docs/v1-harness-design.md calls for returning reviewer findings to the same developer for a bounded number of attempts. It was never implemented: internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go fails the run on any non-approve verdict, and execution.repair_attempts_before_replan is configured, defaulted to 2, and read by nothing. One repair verdict therefore ends the run and requires a human, which is the largest single gap between the harness and the near-autonomous operation the design now states as a goal.

Feed the reviewer's findings back to the developer and re-verify, up to the configured attempt limit, before giving up.
design:
Follow the Work Execution sequence in the design document: on repair, return the findings to the same developer for up to execution.repair_attempts_before_replan attempts (default 2); after the limit, hand control back to the development manager to replan or reassign. That role does not exist yet, so the post-limit path must instead record a durable blocker on the Beads item describing the unresolved findings, rather than silently failing.

Resume the same developer session so the retry keeps its context rather than re-deriving the change from scratch. Every attempt must re-run the deterministic checks and obtain a fresh independent review; an earlier approval must never carry over, and the existing independence evidence (distinct developer and reviewer sessions) must hold on the attempt that ultimately integrates. Preserve the worktree and branch across attempts.

Record the attempt count in durable run state so an interrupted process resumes at the right attempt and cannot exceed the limit by restarting. The reviewer's findings are the developer's input for the next attempt and should be passed as structured findings rather than prose.

TWO CONSTRAINTS FROM A REJECTED FIRST ATTEMPT (run-40b6827595434281826e793db69ac5f2, preserved for reference only at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-2-7/40b68275, commit 5a28d8a). Both were found by the independent reviewer and must not recur:

title: Add the product-manager conversation
description:
Implement 'yoyodyne chat' from the CLI Surface in docs/v1-harness-design.md: an interactive conversation with the product-manager agent, deliberately taken ahead of Milestone 2 artifact governance. The product manager builds its context from the repository's existing Markdown (README.md, docs/) and current Beads state, and discusses product intent with the operator. In this bead it is advisory only: it creates, modifies, and approves nothing. Proposing work is yoyodyne-ifd.4.5.

Chat is not a bounded work item and must not run through the run pipeline: there is no worktree, no deterministic check, no reviewer verdict, and nothing to integrate. It needs its own execution path that reuses the backend, normalized events, and durable state rather than the developer/checks/review/integrate composition.
design: Add an immutable product-manager contract in Go that prefixes the configured persona in the prompt, exactly as developerContract does for the developer, so the bundle persona can specialize how the product manager works but never widen its authority. Reuse the claude-code backend, normalized event stream, and durable run state. Persist the provider session identifier so a conversation resumes across process restarts using the backend's existing --resume support. Keep the persona's stated boundaries enforceable in the contract: the product manager owns product intent rather than implementation, and downstream agents may propose changes to the brief or goals but not make them.

title: Handle concurrent integration contention on a shared target branch
description: Adversarial review of PR #3 traced two runs racing to fast-forward the same target branch. Both promotion paths fail closed under contention -- the in-primary 'git merge --ff-only' hits index lock contention, and the non-checked-out path's 'update-ref' compare-and-swap loses the race on the old-value mismatch -- so no corruption or force-advance is possible. The gap is liveness, not safety: the losing run fails its whole pipeline rather than re-reading the moved target and retrying. Unreachable today because execution.max_concurrent_developers defaults to 1, but it becomes live as soon as this epic raises it.
design:
Settled with the operator 2026-08-18. The losing run retries instead of dying: rebase the worktree onto the moved target, re-run the deterministic checks, obtain a fresh independent review (an earlier approval never carries over -- the reviewed diff changed), and retry the promotion, bounded by a configured attempt limit. A rebase that conflicts is not retried: it is reported as a blocker for reconciliation, never auto-resolved, because the design forbids force-merges and conflict judgment belongs to the development manager -- the operator until that role exists.

This pays before concurrency does: a run already dies today when the operator moves main mid-run, which has happened once this session. Reparented off the scheduler milestone for exactly that reason -- it is integration hardening, not concurrency work.

Retry evidence is durable like repair evidence: attempts recorded before the developer is reinvoked, so a restart cannot buy a fresh budget.
acceptance_criteria: A run that loses an integration race retries or defers instead of failing outright; a test drives two concurrent Integrate calls against one target and asserts exactly one promotion, no lost commit, and no force-advance.

title: Add portable agent defaults and project overrides
description: Replace the bootstrap-only root configuration with a portable project configuration directory and a versioned built-in agent bundle. Yoyodyne must be usable from other project repositories without access to the Yoyodyne source checkout: the executable supplies complete default configurations and personas for product manager, architect, development manager, developer, and reviewer, while each project stores only its machine-independent settings and sparse agent overrides under .yoyodyne/. Add brief override instructions to README.md and a detailed configuration guide under docs/.
design: Embed a read-only builtin:v1 bundle in the executable, represented as declarative configuration and Markdown persona files rather than Go string constants. Keep non-bypassable authority, sandbox, review-verdict, integration, and cleanup rules enforced in Go; configured personas may specialize behavior but cannot remove those invariants. Discover the nearest .yoyodyne/config.yaml from the current directory upward, while continuing to accept an explicit --config path and the legacy .yoyodyne.yaml shape for compatibility. The project config declares extends: builtin:v1 and overlays the built-in bundle by stable agent name. Missing agent fields inherit; supplied scalar fields replace; persona overrides replace the complete inherited persona; instances remain validated; disabled: true explicitly removes an inherited agent; unknown fields, unknown built-in bundles, invalid role/backend combinations, absolute persona paths, traversal, and symlink escape fail closed. Resolve project persona paths within the project .yoyodyne directory, and record enough provenance in the effective config to explain whether a value came from the built-in bundle or project file. Wire effective developer and reviewer personas into their existing prompts without allowing project text into immutable harness policy. Migrate this repository to .yoyodyne/config.yaml and remove .yoyodyne.yaml. Provide config show --effective and --origins output suitable for diagnosing inheritance. Tracked README and docs files follow the repository-document Markdown rules: no ai-output front matter or tl-dr section.

title: An inter-role ask channel: durable, visible, judgment-only exchanges
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-19, adopting the product manager's recommendation. Roles can ask each other questions through the harness - the product manager asking the architect for a cost estimate or a design-intent clarification is the motivating case. Three properties are load-bearing: every exchange is durable and visible, preserving the no-side-conversations property the traceability goal implies; the channel is judgment-only - both conversations are toolless, so an ask moves opinion, never evidence, and verification stays commissioned as developer work (the ifd.97 pattern); and the channel is decisionless - no authority moves through an ask, and decisions still land as amendments, proposals, and directives. The refusal it retires: a one-question exchange currently costs either an operator relay or a full work-item cycle.

The architect designs it.

Operator addition: when the Slack epic lands, inter-role ask exchanges are echoed to Slack so operators can follow the conversation and redirect if needed. Dependency shape: the echo is a consumer of yoyodyne-ifd.68.2's notifier, not a blocker of the channel itself - the channel ships without Slack and gains the echo when the notifier exists.
notes: Operator requirement, 2026-08-19: the channel is explicitly bidirectional, and both directions are first-class in the design with these canonical exchanges recorded as its motivating examples — PM asks architect: 'what does this goal cost, and what am I missing?' (feeding cost and feasibility into backlog ordering before admission); architect asks PM: 'what would the user be impacted by — if we sacrifice some performance, is that an unacceptable trade-off from the user's standpoint?' (feeding user impact into design decisions before they are made, rather than as findings after). The judgment-only, decisionless, durable-and-visible properties apply identically in both directions, as does the Slack echo once 68.2's notifier exists. Second operator requirement, same date: a configurable hard limit on rounds per exchange thread — default 10, validated at least 1, durable with the exchange so a process death cannot reset it (the repair-budget pattern). Hitting the cap is not a silent cutoff: the exchange closes as unresolved-after-N-rounds and escalates to the operator as a question or report, converting the pathological two-judgment-models-deferring-forever loop into a rare legible operator question. Per-exchange cost is reported beside the rounds so the operator sees what a conversation spent (ties to the cost goal).

title: Gate developer diffs on protected paths, deterministically, before review
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-19. Protected paths - .yoyodyne/**, docs/product/**, docs/designs/**, docs/decisions/** - are default-deny for a developer's diff: refused before review like a failing check and handed back inside the existing repair loop, unless the work item explicitly grants the path, so every exception is declared in reviewed item text rather than discovered as surprise. The refusal names the grant mechanism, so a developer that genuinely needs a path raises it instead of sneaking it.

Rationale for the record: closes the design's one admitted gap - an agent with an editor in its worktree - deterministically. Today that class costs an Opus review cycle to catch; ifd.70's scope-creep refusal burned two repairs and $18 reaching a conclusion this gate reaches free. It is the checks-expansion lever in its purest form: a class of reviewer finding retired into a gate.

title: Surface failed runs and their reasons through a yoyo verb
description: The write side of failure persistence is solid: a terminal run's record keeps status, the phase it died in, and the failure message coherently (23 such records on disk, from full review verdicts to 'primary checkout is not ready for integration'), with separated companions — check_failure, publish_failure, cleanup_failure, completion_recording_failure — so bookkeeping failures cannot masquerade as run failures, and the same reason lands in the work item's notes. title: Decide how directory indexes and out-of-home identity are governed
description: Two blind spots ifd.1.9's developer verified: (1) a README inside an artifact home can never be governed — the store skips readme.md by name and README fails the id pattern, frontmatter on one is inert — yet docs/product/goals/README.md carries normative prose teaching the goal-writing contract, invisible to reference checking, staleness, and the amendment channel; (2) a document carrying artifact frontmatter OUTSIDE every configured home is invisible rather than reported — the store never walks it, the load stays clean, it looks governed while nothing downstream can refer to it, which is exactly how v1-harness-design sat ungoverned with no check catching it. ifd.1.9 adds a repository-level test guarding docs/, but the harness itself still reports nothing. The architect decides: indexes get identity or their normative prose moves into governed artifacts, and whether the store reports stray identity. Architect arrives with ifd.4.
notes:
The architect decided both halves in its first session (chat-11558d32), so this item is now implementation of a recorded decision, not an open question: (1) indexes stay ungoverned — README.md by name, navigation not authority, and a governed index would be stale by construction — with normative prose moving out: the mechanically checked shape into a governed architect-owned specification of the artifact contract, the qualities-of-a-good-goal guidance into the PM's own goals documents, the index keeping pointers; (2) stray identity is reported by the harness, bounded to parent directories of the configured homes (docs/ in the default layout, fixtures and vendored trees excluded by that bound), README frontmatter reported as inert in the same channel, reported never refused. The decision record and specification revision are part of this item's delivery.
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 79.

Reason: Both halves are chain integrity: normative prose invisible to reference checking and amendment is intent outside the chain, and artifact frontmatter outside every governed home is identity the chain cannot see. The architect's recorded decisions make this implementation of exactly that goal.

Goal served: Maintain a traceable chain from the product brief through goals, designs, work, code changes, and verification.

title: Expand declared checks to retire recurring reviewer findings
description: Lever 2 of the token-efficiency brainstorm (ai-output/2026-08-18-token-efficiency-levers.md): every mechanical defect a deterministic check catches is attention the reviewer does not spend, and the candidates come from our own report stream — (a) a goals-file lint enforcing one physical line per goal statement (the 0n1 class); (b) a documentation link checker for the reference problems the artifact layer already warns about; (c) the dispatcher-coverage test suggested by ifd.70's reviewer is deliberately NOT here — it is ifd.81's second half, referenced to avoid duplication. Detecting negative impact: (1) false positives — the run records keep every check's pass/fail per verify pass; a bad check is one that fails often while the diffs fixing it are trivial appeasement churn, versus a good check's signature of rare failures with real causes; (2) runtime drag — checks run on every verify pass including each repair, so wall-clock per check (recorded, timeouts configurable per ifd.56) multiplies; an expensive check needs to earn it; (3) reviewer complacency — invisible in check data, visible in the escaped-defect rate: bugs filed in beads against already-merged work, the backstop metric for any quality-affecting change; (4) the findings channel itself — developers report checks that fight them, as this week's reports demonstrated. Operator-approved 2026-08-18.

title: Audit prompt assembly for prefix stability so provider caching pays
description: Lever 5 of the token-efficiency brainstorm (ai-output/2026-08-18-token-efficiency-levers.md). Provider prompt caching pays when the immutable contract + persona + invariants prefix is byte-stable across turns and sessions; audit prompt assembly in the pipeline so nothing volatile — run ids, timestamps, per-run paths — appears before the stable prefix, reordering only, never removing. Detecting impact, both directions: (1) effect — the cache-read share of input tokens (already in the provider usage records yoyo cost prices) must rise after the change; if it does not, the change failed at its purpose and is reverted as a null result; (2) harm — compare a ~20-run window before and after on first-pass approval rate, repair attempts per landed item, and cost per landed item, all already durable in run records; staleness specifically would surface as review findings citing repo-state mismatches that were not real; (3) guard — land with a test pinning that dynamic content (context bundle, item description) still appears in assembled prompts, so a stable prefix cannot quietly become a frozen prompt. Operator-approved 2026-08-18.

description: Lever 7 of the token-efficiency brainstorm (ai-output/2026-08-18-token-efficiency-levers.md), scheduled first because every other efficiency lever is tuned blind without it. title: Team mode: collaborators each run yoyo against one shared repository
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-18. Collaborators download yoyo and run it against the shared repository. The git/forge layer already survives multiple committers - namespaced run branches, branch protection, drift replay with fresh verdicts - and the supported answer today is one harness plus friends as ordinary committers. What breaks when each person runs their own harness is the coordination layer, single-operator throughout. Five recorded gaps bound the scope: (1) the tracker diverges per machine - Beads syncs via a Dolt remote on the git remote, nothing configures it, every bd call warns; (2) no distributed claim - two machines can claim one item in the sync window and one loses after paying for development and review; (3) the one-promotion-per-target-branch lease is machine-scoped flock, so across machines the invariant silently narrows and the forge is the only backstop; (4) report stores, run state, product-manager conversations, and the pause switch are per-machine - findings and control do not travel; (5) operator identity is recorded without proof, the forgeability gap already a design precondition on ifd.25, multiplied across humans whose intent can conflict.

Scope questions this epic answers: what team mode promises, who counts as an operator, whether one-harness-many-committers is the supported v1 answer. Sequencing decided by the operator: the product manager's scoping document first; the architecture pass waits for the architect role ifd.4 creates, with the explicit constraint that operator identity is designed once, jointly for ifd.25's precondition and this epic, not twice.

RECONCILIATION PENDING: the team goal this epic names is drafted but not yet in v1-goals.md, and v1-non-goals.md still records multiple human users as a v1 non-goal - both need the operator's pen. This attribution was accepted while goal validation is down (empty artifact store, see the warning filed on 2026-08-18) and must be verified when ifd.1.9 seeds the goals.

title: Document the contributor workflow the harness already supports: local-only .yoyodyne via .git/info/exclude and --config
description: A contributor to a repository they do not own may not want to commit tool-specific configuration. Two existing mechanisms already cover this and neither is documented: the harness discovers .yoyodyne from the launch checkout's disk regardless of git tracking, so listing it in .git/info/exclude (the personal ignore file that is never committed) keeps it invisible to upstream while everything runs; and every command accepts --config for a directory outside the repo entirely. Add a README section for this workflow, with the caveats: nothing inside a dev worktree can see the config (today nothing needs to), and the project stops being self-describing for other machines — which is the point in this scenario. Operator-approved 2026-08-19.

title: Warn when .yoyodyne is gitignored, in init and config validate
description: A newcomer who reflexively gitignores tool config gets no error and eventual drift: the launch checkout keeps working from disk, but clones and collaborators get an unconfigured project, and dev worktrees (which check out tracked files only) silently lack the directory. yoyo init and yoyo config validate should check whether .yoyodyne is matched by the repository's ignore rules (git check-ignore) and say plainly what committing it means: the project stops being self-describing for every other machine. The warning should acknowledge the legitimate case — a contributor who cannot commit tool config to someone else's repository — and point at the supported alternative rather than just scolding (today that is --config or a .git/info/exclude local ignore; a first-class external-config mode is under exploration by the operator). Approved by the operator 2026-08-18.

title: Close a superseded pull request when its work lands by another vehicle
description: When integration abandons the pull request a run opened — the approved work lands instead through a conflict-resolution replay (ifd.1.5: PR #44 superseded by PR #46) or a hand recovery (ifd.1.7: PR #45, integrated directly) — nothing closes the original. It sits open with a green build and no auto-merge, indistinguishable from pending work until a human asks why. The publish phase should close the superseded PR with a comment naming where the work actually landed (the superseding PR or the integrating commit), so the forge's open-PR list stays an honest picture of what is pending. Found by the operator noticing PRs #44 and #45 open days after both beads closed.
notes:
Root cause found: not the conflict-replay path. Both orphans are publications of dead first runs whose items were relaunched after the SIGTERM incident. PR #44 = ifd.1.5 run c25525d6, superseded by run e978c992 / PR #46; PR #45 = ifd.1.7 run af68c66f, superseded by run f931d78f / PR #47. Branch names embed the run id, so a relaunch publishes a new branch and a new PR, and nothing revisits the dead run's publications. Fix belongs in reconcile, not publish: run state records the pull request and the worktree interface already has DeleteRemoteBranch, so when reconcile finds a terminal run whose item was completed by another run, close the recorded PR with a comment naming the superseding PR or integrating commit, and delete the dead remote branch. The operator wants this fixed, not just recorded. Interim state: both PRs were closed by hand on 2026-08-18 with comments naming their successors, but the remote branches (yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-1-5/c25525d6, yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-1-7/af68c66f) and the preserved local worktrees still exist — deleting them is this item's job, and the ifd-1-5 worktree is checked out on its branch, so branch deletion must release or prune the worktree first.
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 64.

Reason: The forge's open-PR list staying an honest picture of pending work is this goal's hygiene: a superseded publication nothing closes is harness-opened publishing leaving a false signal. The reconcile-side fix closes the loop the goal opened.

Goal served: Publish that work as pull requests the harness opens, and has the forge merge, on the roles' behalf, for projects that enable it, without letting any agent push or merge.

title: Show the recently shipped work with its price and its wall clock
description:
The operator wants one call that answers what shipped lately and what it took: yoyo status listing the n most recently shipped work items, each with its provider-reported cost and the wall-clock time from claim to promotion.

Cost attribution already exists: ifd.41 records provider-reported cost per item across every run made for it, and yoyo cost reports it. What is missing is the time dimension and the ledger view -- most-recent-first, bounded, glanceable.

yoyo status is also the verb the design document has always listed for the CLI and never built; the conversation's /status covers in-flight work. This item may introduce the command with shipped work as its first section, or extend yoyo cost -- implementer's call, stated with reasoning, but the operator asked for it as yoyo status.
design:
Wall clock is two honest numbers, not one. Elapsed from first claim to promotion includes usage-limit pauses, which on 2026-08-17 were hours of the night; the pause seconds are already durable per run (usage_limit_paused_seconds). Report elapsed and paused side by side so a four-hour item that spent three parked reads as what it was. Sum across every run the item took, including failed and discarded attempts, consistent with ifd.41's accounting: the honest time includes rework.

Timestamps come from what is already recorded -- the tracker's started/closed times and the runs' started/completed times -- rather than new bookkeeping. An item whose runs predate some of the recording reports what it can and marks the rest unknown, never zero, per ifd.41's rule.

Output is a table: item, title, cost, elapsed, paused, runs, most recent first, default n around ten, machine-readable with --json like everything else.
acceptance_criteria: One command lists the n most recently shipped items with provider-reported cost, elapsed wall clock, and paused time, most recent first; totals across the listing are shown; unknowns are stated as unknown rather than zero; --json works; the choice of verb (yoyo status or an extension of yoyo cost) is recorded with its reasoning; the conversation's /status is unchanged.

description: Before max_concurrent_developers rises above one anywhere by default, drive two real work items concurrently and verify the claims under contention rather than asserting them: reservation and capacity under two live claims, the promotion lease serializing two integrations, two pull requests racing auto-merge, two runs pausing on the shared five-hour window and both resuming, a paused run correctly holding its capacity slot, and reconcile with two outstanding runs at once. Same discipline as the non-Go fixture: the configuration flip is trivial, the proof is the work.
acceptance_criteria: Two concurrent runs on distinct items both land end to end with promotions serialized; shared-window pauses on both runs resume correctly; reconcile settles a deliberately interrupted pair; findings from the soak are filed as beads; the observed behaviors are recorded on this item as the evidence for raising the default.

SOAK EVIDENCE, 2026-08-18, attempt log:

- Shared five-hour window: two developers drained it roughly twice as fast; both runs recorded the same 18:50Z deadline and parked; both would have resumed unaided. Confirms concurrency is limit-bound before it is CPU-bound.
- Operator release gap: capacity purchased mid-wait had no verb; manual release required kill+reconcile+reopen and redevelopment. SIGTERM lands as terminal cancelled with the item still claimed. -> ifd.53 (probe-under-deadline + release verb).
- Provider overload storm: 529s failed runs outright after the CLI's ten internal retries; the harness had no wait for transient server refusal. -> ifd.54.
- Check timeout under contention: two concurrent make test suites exceeded the flat ten-minute check timeout while passing; good work failed at verification. -> ifd.56. Checks are the second wall-clock kill, one layer below the provider timeout fixed in ifd.30.
- Chat during two runs: a product-manager turn completed normally alongside two live developers.
- Promotion lease: NOT yet exercised under real contention -- no attempt has had two simultaneous promotions; remains the open observation for the next clean attempt.

FINAL EVIDENCE, 2026-08-18 afternoon: the clean attempt exercised everything. Two runs held concurrent claims; ifd.1.7 completed end to end and self-merged (pull request 47) while its sibling worked; ifd.1.5, already reviewer-approved, hit the moved target, attempted the replay ifd.3.1 built, met a genuine three-file conflict (both items added fields at the same seams), and refused to auto-resolve exactly as designed -- conflict named, work preserved, nothing force-merged. title: Mark downstream artifacts and work stale when an upstream artifact changes
description:
When a goal changes, the designs that serve it and the work that traces to it may no longer be right, and nothing says so. Today a goal can be amended while work built on the old wording continues to completion, and the divergence is found by a person or not at all. Propagate staleness downstream when an artifact changes.

DONE: amending an artifact marks the artifacts and open work items downstream of it as stale; staleness is visible to the operator and names what changed upstream; staleness is recorded durably rather than held in a running process.

CONSTRAINT: stale is not cancelled. Marking work stale must not stop or discard it - a change to a goal's wording is frequently not a change to what the work should do, and a system that discards work on every edit teaches operators not to edit. What happens to stale work is a decision for the operator or the owning role, and this item surfaces the condition rather than acting on it.

title: Pause the work a directive affects when the directive is ambiguous or changes an artifact
description:
ifd.1's acceptance criteria require that the harness pauses affected work for ambiguous or artifact-changing directives. Today a directive that changes what an in-flight item should do does not reach that item; work continues against the intent it was given. Reconcile a new directive against work already in flight and pause what it affects.

DONE: a directive that changes a governed artifact, or that is ambiguous enough to need the operator, pauses the work items it affects rather than only being recorded; the pause names the directive and what is unresolved; work resumes when the ambiguity is answered or the artifact change is decided; a directive reaches the work it affects regardless of which agent received it.

CONSTRAINT: pause, do not cancel, and settle what a paused run leaves behind exactly as stopping already does rather than abandoning it. The failure to design against is a directive that is durably recorded and reaches nothing, which is the state today - recording a directive is not enforcing one.

title: Let a role propose a change to an artifact it does not own
description:
Once ownership is enforced, a role that needs an upstream artifact changed has no way to say so. The escalation path is already described: a developer proposes an upstream change, the architect evaluates it and owns the design amendment, and only an unworkable goal reaches the product manager. Build the mechanism that carries a proposed change from a non-owner to the owner and the operator.

DONE: a role can propose a change to an artifact it does not own; the proposal reaches the artifact's owner and the operator with what is proposed and why; the owner or the operator decides, and only that decision writes; a proposal is durable rather than lost when the run that raised it ends.

CONSTRAINT: reuse the proposal and decision path yoyodyne-ifd.24 already built for work items rather than building a second one. A proposal is never a deferred edit - nothing an unapproved proposal contains reaches the artifact. Do not let a proposal mechanism become a way for a downstream role to change upstream intent slowly.

DECOMPOSITION NOTE: created by the product manager under operator authorization 2026-08-17, because no development manager exists yet - the role arrives with yoyodyne-ifd.4, which yoyodyne-ifd.1 gates. Decomposition belongs to the development manager; this shape should be re-derived or ratified when the role runs. Do not start before the ownership enforcement child lands.

title: Let a conversation turn wait out a usage limit the way a run does
description:
A run that hits a provider usage limit records the reset time, pauses, and resumes; a conversation turn that hits one simply fails. Observed 2026-08-17: turn 13 of the product-manager conversation performed seven tracker reads, delivered its reply preamble, and then died with 'You've hit your session limit, resets 8:30pm' when the continuation invocation was refused -- the ifd.1 decomposition it was about to create never happened, and the operator asking 'did we stop?' is what surfaced it.

The machinery exists: the rate-limit envelope is parsed, the reset time is known, and runs already wait bounded intervals against a budget. Conversations bypass all of it.
design: Reuse the run behavior rather than inventing a second one: on an exhausted limit with a reset time inside the in-process bound, wait and reissue the turn; past the bound or with no reset time, follow the same rules runs follow. The turn's partial work is already durable -- tracker actions applied before the failure stay applied, which is correct and should be stated: a reissued turn continues a session that already holds them. Interactive mode should show the wait through the activity display rather than sitting silent, and --message mode should wait the same way since an unattended caller is exactly who cannot retry by hand.
acceptance_criteria: A conversation turn that hits a waitable usage limit waits and completes rather than failing; the wait is visible in interactive mode and bounded by the same configuration runs use; tracker actions applied before the pause are not repeated after it; an unwaitable limit fails with the reset information stated; a test replays the limit-then-reset sequence against a fake backend.
notes: Fresh evidence 2026-08-18: a chat --message turn failed outright with 'product manager reported failure: api_error' where a run would have waited and retried. The turn was retried by hand and the operator's agent lost nothing, but the asymmetry the bead describes is now demonstrated on the PM's own conversation, not just predicted.
